[Mr. Garson.l

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Before the hon. member begins his remarks, may I say that I would not want the action I have taken today to be considered as a precedent, since it is contrary to other precedents in this house.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house and the people generally will be glad that you have permitted this motion to be moved today.
There is great concern across the country following the announcement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) permitting another- and I emphasize the word "another"-and drastic increase in domestic rents-without, incidentally, any appeal to any body for the purpose of determining whether or not there is justice in that increase. I am glad, too, you did not hold that this question might be discussed in the budget debate, because I would remind hon. members that that debate is partly concluded, and some hon. members who might have liked to discuss this matter would be precluded from doing so because they have exhausted their right to speak.
Of course I readily admit that the policy announced by the Minister of Finance was in line with the general policy of decontrol instituted by the government after the war. We hold the view that the removal of beneficial controls and subsidies following the war has resulted in the cost of living in this country reaching unprecedented heights. The government may say that this was all done before the last general election, and that therefore this policy was approved by the electors of

Canada on June 27 last, when they gave the government the green light to proceed with its policies. But I do not believe the people thought the government would allow drastic increases in domestic rents before something had been done to provide housing accommodation, which would be within the reach of great masses of the Canadian people. If the view is taken, as is sometimes put forward, that the people of Canada supported the policy laid down by the government in these particulars, then all I can say is that many of the people of Canada who are complaining today are getting precisely what they voted for. I am convinced, though, that had many thousands of Canadians realized that within five months of the election further increases of twenty and twenty-five per cent in rents would be announced, the government would not have had the huge following in this house which it has today. Hundreds of thousands of families are paying rents for inadequate accommodation far beyond their means. Overcrowding in every part of Canada, particularly in every large urban centre, is, I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me, the order of the day. Low-income groups are paying rents far beyond their capacity.
No provision in the way of low rental accommodation has been made for hundreds of thousands of families who have no veteran under their roof. Let us not forget that. It was our obligation to make every possible provision for the veterans who served this country in the last war. But there are many thousands of men and women engaged in industry, who stayed in industry in order to serve their country during that great struggle, and for them no provision has been made. It has been estimated by the Community Planning Association of Canada that there are a half million tenant families in Canada who can afford no more, and many indeed much less, than $30 a month for shelter. This I presume is based on the government's own advice, given several years ago to our people, that no more than twenty per cent of the family income should be expended for shelter. Many families in Canada today are compelled to pay from forty to fifty per cent of the family income for shelter.
The shortage of houses is not a new thing in this country. For many years in every part of Canada thousands of families were awaiting housing accommodation, on a rental basis, which they could not get. There were more families than there was housing or shelter accommodation to provide for them. I recall an interesting debate in this house on February 17, 1936, in which the deplorable housing conditions revealed by the 1931 census were discussed. I participated in that debate,
Rent Control
which was initiated by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I recall that I drew attention to the fact that there were thousands of members of the building trades idle at that time. It was a time, as hon. members will recall, of serious unemployment in this country. The lumbering industry was suffering from serious unemployment and a lack of markets. The manufacturers of building materials and other supplies required in the erection of homes were maintaining idle plants while there were many thousands of Canadians on relief.
In other words, we had the resources; we had the artisans; we had the lumber and the factories to produce all we needed in order to build houses. Nothing was done. Thousands of our young men were idling in relief camps at twenty cents a day. Had we had the policy this country should have had at that time under a Liberal administration, and the year before under a Conservative administration, we could have utilized the materials, resources and human labour forces in such a way as to make some provision for the houses that were lacking in 1931 and the years before.
During those depression years, Mr. Speaker, the governments of the day did nothing effective to promote the building of houses. In other countries, nation-wide projects were undertaken, notably by the newly-elected Labour government of New Zealand; by the government of Sweden; by the government of the United Kingdom, and by the governments of the other civilized countries. If hon. gentlemen will look at the census reports for 1941, particularly volume 9 at page 182, they will find that the census returns show that 18-1 per cent of the housing units were overcrowded, and that 978,227 Canadians were living under overcrowded conditions.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: How many were empty at that time?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I do not know how many were empty. There may have been some empty houses. If there were empty houses in 1941, Mr. Speaker, two years after the war broke out, it underlines the fact that in 1940 and 1941 thousands of persons were unemployed in this country. In the first year of war there were approximately 400,000 persons unemployed and on relief. These deplorable conditions continued until the destruction of war enabled employment to become widespread, improve Canadian farm prices, and pull us out of a depression we had not managed to get out of under a Liberal administration in all the years that went before. I should add that neither the labour nor the materials were available in 1941 and the war years that followed.

Rent Control
The government points, of course, with pride to what has been done since the war ended. A number of new housing units have been built. But let me point this out. Equally important is the kind of house that can be bought or rented by families- whether they are accessible to the wealthy few or the less wealthy many. Judged by this standard, the housing policy of the government since the war has failed. Judged by this standard, the consternation of many people who suffer from inflated rents, and those who view with misgivings the possibility of further wage demands and salary increases, cannot be ignored.
I have already said that overcrowding persists in this country. Let us remember that overcrowding, resulting in large measure from high rents and high prices, will ultimately have a serious effect upon the health of the people generally. With the greater proportion of the family income absorbed in payment for shelter, it will undoubtedly mean a lowering of food standards. When food standards are lowered and supplies of milk for the family have to be reduced, physical deterioration of many families follows.
Let us remember that tens of thousands of houses and apartments built since the war, with the exception of those made available to veterans-and I am glad that lower rental accommodation is available to veterans-are renting today at $50, $60, and $70 or more per month. Indeed, this is not only permitted but encouraged under the government's housing plans. The guarantees offered to private builders have resulted in the building of apartments to rent, in most cases at not less than $70 a month. When rentals as high as this are asked, invariably the landlords say that this figure has been approved by the government of Canada. The dominion bureau of statistics reported that in 1948 thousands of urban families in rented shelters were paying no more than $30 a month; but when we examine the kind of accommodation they had at that rate, we see that they were in overcrowded rooms, overcrowded housekeeping rooms, overcrowded small houses, and that overcrowded conditions prevailed generally among that group of people. For this important group of Canadian families, which, again according to the bureau of statistics, is about one in every four, little housing has been built since the beginning of the great depression in the 1930's.
A large proportion of the Canadian people have been left entirely out of the picture since the war, because the government's policy has not resulted in the building of housing units within their reach. Now, before making any provision for this group, the government announces a drastic increase in
[Mr. ColdwellJ
rents, twenty per cent for unheated units and twenty-five per cent for heated units. This is a substantial increase, following, as it does, three previous increases of five, ten and four per cent respectively. It should be remembered that those increases, together with the twenty per cent or twenty-five per cent now, will mean an increase of forty per cent or more since the end of world war II.
No doubt some landlords have been receiving rental returns that are inadequate; but had we continued a proper rent control system, these surely could have been adjusted. This cannot, however, justify the government's announcement of the large increases that were announced last week. There can be no excuse for permitting at this time increases as much as twenty and twenty-five per cent all round.
One has only to consult the advertising columns of the newspapers in any city-in Ottawa, if you will-to realize the heights to which lack of accommodation and competition for new-occupancy dwellings have forced rents. In one of the local papers a couple of weeks ago a two-bedroom bungalow was advertised for rent, unfurnished, at $125 a month. A census of overcrowding in the urban centres of Canada would indicate that thousands of families are living under conditions that are intolerable, and for inadequate accommodation, are paying rents that can only be described as extortionate. Yet now the government allows a further increase of twenty-five per cent or twenty per cent, which will only aggravate the intolerable conditions to which I have referred.
This house, Mr. Speaker, must say explicitly to the government that the recent announcement of the Minister of Finance must be reconsidered and that rental controls must remain until the provinces are prepared to step into the field and undertake the protection of the Canadian people, if it should prove to be their obligation to do so. Indeed, until the menace of high rentals has been removed, the government, in its reconsideration of this policy, at least should provide for appeals to rental control boards across the country before rent increases are put into effect, and indicate that they should apply not only with respect to houses that have been under rental control, but also to some of these new occupancy dwellings and apartments as well.
I know that this is a problem which affects the urban members of this house more directly than it affects the rural members, but I appeal to all hon. members to join in this protest. The announcement of the Minister of Finance shows an entire disregard of the welfare of the great masses of the Canadian people, and this should not be

tolerated by the house. I only wish it were possible at this time to move an amendment to test the feeling of the house and that hon. members in all parts of the house would feel free to vote for such an amendment on the merits of the case.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, a motion was offered to you for the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing this subject. At that time your ruling was that the subject could be discussed during the course of the day, on the motion to go into committee of supply, and therefore you did not permit discussion of the subject. I had assumed that had the question arisen today, your ruling would have been that the subject might be discussed on the bill to amend the National Housing Act, which is to be considered at a later stage of today's proceedings.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We could not take a chance on that.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, you have permitted debate to proceed on this motion, and I should like to contribute some thoughts with reference to this subject of rent control, particularly in the light of the announcement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in this house on Thursday night last.
It seems to me to be a most anomalous situation that we have two ministers, one of whom, the Minister of Finance, is responsible for administration of all aspects of the housing problem that fall under the subject of rent control, or the controlling powers of the wartime prices and trade board, and another, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), who is supposed to be responsible for all matters in which the federal authority is interested that fall under the subject matter of housing. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is responsible for administration of the National Housing Act. Here we have a dual system, with one minister not in a position to announce policy in a field that falls within the province of the other, and creating confusion in debates in the house, and also in government policy and government administration. It seems to me that in the proceedings of this house yesterday and today, as well as last week, we have had clear evidence that this dual system should not be allowed to continue. It is high time that the government made up its mind to unify its program and policy, if any, with reference to housing. You cannot take out of the field of housing this question of rent control or freezing controls on tenant-occupied accommodation and treat that matter as though
Rent Control
it were a problem separate and apart from the problem of the housing needs of the Canadian people.
Rent controls became necessary because of a critical scarcity of housing. A critical scarcity of housing came about partly because of wartime conditions and partly because of deliberate government policy. In this respect I do not dissociate government policy from the conduct of the war, but I say that this scarcity, which has existed for some years now, and still exists in critical proportions, is attributable to government policy, for it became government policy during the war to remove much of the productive capacity of the building and construction industry from its normal pursuits and to devote it to war production. Labour was siphoned off from the construction trades, and the scarcity of housing continued to accumulate. Because we had an abnormal situation it became the duty of the government to step into this field and to take measures to control rents and to impose certain freezing regulations, simply because these measures were necessary to cope with the scarcity, an abnormal situation itself directly attributable to government policy.
What is the background? What are the conditions from which this new statement of government policy made by the Minister of Finance stems? It certainly does not stem from a situation in which the problem of scarcity has been corrected. It does not stem from an abundance of housing in Canada. The conditions out of which, the background against which, this last announcement of government policy has been made are conditions as critical as at any time in the past. Sir, I am not going to repeat what I said on this subject in the house on October 31, but I do remind hon. members, every one of whom has a responsibility in the light of this new statement of government policy, to consider facts such as these: first, that Mr. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, said last January:
The number of household groups, including not only families but also individuals who maintain households, exceed the number of front doors by approximately 350,000.
And again, the statement of General Young, vice-president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, made on April 28:
Canada's housing situation is getting worse instead of better.
And the statement of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply of recent date:
New housing, even at the present record rate of production, is barely keeping up with current needs and making no important inroads into the backlog.

Rent Control
That, sir, is the background. That, sir, is the state of affairs out of which the government has enunciated a new policy of permitting increases in controlled rents, extending up to twenty-five per cent across the board.
It needs to be said, and said most emphatically, that this announcement represents a government decision, and a decision by the government alone. Parliament has had no voice whatever in the new order that has been made. Parliament has not been consulted in any way. The Minister of Finance simply came into the house and announced a fait accompli. He merely acquainted the house with the fact that the government, by executive decree, had imposed these increases ranging up to twenty-five per cent.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No landlord has to charge them.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we had some enlightening comments from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a few days ago on the subject of naivete. I think that the Minister of Finance has broken all records for naivete in the statement he has just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
And, sir, the position in which parliament is left in dealing with a subject of this kind is a most uncomfortable and inconvenient one, because all that parliament can do now is to discuss something that has already been decided. Of course, if it ever came to a question of voting on this, the Minister of Finance would be rising in his place, as he did only yesterday, and saying: Well, there may be something in this argument that has been made from various quarters of the house, but this motion comes from the opposition; therefore it becomes a test of confidence in the government, and therefore I reject the motion or the amendment. Then the government members are called upon to fall in line, because the Minister of Finance says it becomes a test of confidence in the government.
Well, sir, in the form in which this matter comes before the house today we have not even the opportunity of introducing an amendment or a motion. That is most unfortunate, and for that very reason it seems to me more incumbent upon any government supporters in the house, who are not prepared to swallow this government announcement whole, to rise in their places and say so, and not to follow along like driven sheep simply because the Minister of Finance says it is government policy.
Sir, nothing could have been more arbitrary than the way in which this increase has been brought about-no consultation with parliament, no opportunity on the part

of parliament to investigate the matter; simply an executive order more far-reaching, I venture to say, in its effect on the homes of Canadians throughout this broad land than anything else that has been done or transacted or said in this parliament throughout the present session.
It is an amazing thing that while parliament is in session the thing which has affected the lives and homes of Canadians more than any other since this session began was something done outside parliament, and parliament is simply notified at quarter to eleven one evening that it has been done. Moreover, it will continue to be possible for the government, simply by such executive decrees, without consulting this parliament, to make sweeping changes that affect Canadian homes by the hundreds of thousands, if we permit the government to enjoy the powers that they possess today under the Transitional Measures Act. This points, as clearly as anything can possibly point, to the inherent error in the way in which parliament has clothed this government with powers in view of the alleged national emergency. I am not going to retrace the whole ground covered in the debate of the first 1949 session, when we of the official opposition pointed the way to the government as to the method which ought to be taken in laying a proper legislative groundwork for rent control. But, of course, the government were not accepting suggestions of that kind. Rather they insisted on arrogating to themselves those wide omnibus powers under the Transitional Measures Act, and then by executive decree making the sweeping orders under the powers conferred by that act.
I wish to place before the new members of the house one or two extracts from significant passages in the debate on that measure. I recall two important remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in the debate. First of all I shall quote his statement of March 14, 1949, when at page 1446 of Hansard he said:
The time has come for the government to place before parliament a statute dealing with the housing problem, and to provide in that statute clear and unmistakable terms which can be understood by both landlords and tenants so the confusion which exists today may be brought to an end.
I would have thought that that was a very constructive suggestion, but the government rejected it. They wanted an omnibus bill giving them sweeping powers, and then under that measure to have the power by executive decree to make orders such as the one which was announced by the minister on Thursday night. Sir, can you imagine anything that contributes more to chaos and confusion, as well as to hardship, in Canadian homes today

Rent Control
than this continued uncertainty as to when another executive order is to be made? People are simply at the mercy of executive orders; for these orders are made whether parliament is in session or parliament is not in session. Their elected representatives do not control the situation. Their elected representatives, by reason of the nature of the legislation under which these orders are made, have not had any voice whatever in the making of the decisions embodied in this order.
At page 1448 of Hansard of the same date the leader of the opposition said:
I hope that no one will suggest that any hon. member who opposes the continuance of these wartime powers is opposing rent control or any other provision to meet the situation which has arisen very largely as a result of the activities of the government itself.
We Progressive Conservatives said that the measure embodying this omnibus power was an inherently wrong method, and asked the government to bring in a proper measure to embody the legislative provisions needed with respect to the relationship between landlord and tenant in this emergency situation.
At page 1484 I had some comments to make -and I mention these with diffidence and simply because it fell to my lot to follow my leader in the debate. Hansard of March 15, 1949, page 1484, contains my following words:
It was made quite clear by my leader in his remarks yesterday that an adverse vote on this omnibus resolution by any member of this party-
The Progressive Conservative party.
-is not to be considered as opposition to rent control, a proper statutory measure of rent control. That has been made abundantly clear by the observations of the leader of the opposition at pages 1446 and 1448 of Hansard yesterday, so let there be no misunderstanding of the attitude of the members of this official opposition, of which I think we had a veiled suggestion last evening in the question asked by a member to your right, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of rent control. It has to be a proper measure; it has to be a measure in proper statutory form, not something hidden in an omnibus resolution of this kind.
We followed that up; and when the bill to continue the Transitional Measures Act came before the house for second reading we offered an amendment which is to be found at page 1743 of Hansard for 1949.
This was the amendment introduced by the official opposition to the motion for second reading:
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to recommend a specific measure relating to rent control, and other specific measures relating respectively to other matters provided for in the said bill.
After some discussion, Mr. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order, the house
dividing on our appeal from the ruling. The ruling was upheld, and the division is recorded at page 1766 of Hansard.
I now turn to some of the features of the statement of the Minister of Finance on Thursday night. He has announced that the government proposes a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine the constitutionality of federal rent control. If doubts have been raised, I suppose it is desirable that this matter be settled in that way. I think it might be asked, however, and with some justification, why that course was not followed earlier; because had there been a decision earlier on that question by the Supreme Court of Canada it certainly would have enabled us to know even at this stage the position with reference to the powers of parliament. Even if a favourable decision had been made as long ago as a year, it is reasonable to expect that the judges of the supreme court would have indicated the formula by which the emergency in this respect is to be tested, under which the dominion would derive its power. However, that aspect of the announcement will probably be generally approved.
I turn now to the specific increases made by executive order, and I ask members of the House of Commons what their position is in the light of these measures. It is not an answer for any member of the house-least of all, members supporting the government- to say: Oh, well; that was done by the government under special power, and did not come directly before the house in any manner which would have permitted action by the house. That would be turning our backs upon our responsibility; it would be an endeavour to escape responsibilities which the house must meet, in the face of this government's decisions.
Apparently parliament is not to be afforded any opportunity to review the evidence upon which the government proceeded to make its order. The government has refused to allow the house to appoint a select committee to review housing conditions in this country, or to consider such evidence as the rent control authorities have, and upon which they based their recommendations to the government now embodied in this cabinet decree.
Has there been any progress in decontrol? The house would like to know. We had a statement from the government on October 3, in reply to some questions asked with a view to eliciting information as to the progress which had been made under previous rent control amending orders. At page 442 of Hansard we see that the order of April 14, 1947, concerning landlords who suffered grievous hardship from their inability to recover

Rent Control
possession of their own housing accommodation, permitted recovery of possession in a total of 8,388 cases up to August 31, 1949.
Then, under another rent control order effective November 1, 1948, the wartime prices and trade board permitted landlords who needed housing accommodation for their own personal residence, and who had owned it since November 1, 1947, to give to the tenant six months' notice to vacate. The government reported at page 442 of Hansard of the present session that up to August 31, 1948, such notices had been filed to a total of 9,900. I do not know whether that should be the year 1949; I daresay the "1948" is a mistake. The filing of notices does not signify that those landlords recovered possession of their houses.
That is about all the information given to the house on the subject. It is on that inadequate information that the members of the House of Commons will have to accept and swallow the government's decision, or say, as I hope they will say: We are not satisfied with this. As a matter of fact, more information came out in this morning's press than members of the House of Commons have been given in the house-and more than they would have had opportunity to obtain, I am sure, so long as we are to be denied any opportunity to appoint a committee of the house to consider these questions and to adduce firsthand evidence.
A Canadian Press dispatch appearing in this morning's press contains just about all the information available to us on the subject. It states:
The boost in rental ceilings which comes into effect ten days before Christmas may hit some 4 million Canadians living in rented rooms, flats, apartments and houses, government officials estimated today.
The official based this estimate on a rental survey which showed that approximately 1,500,000 flats, apartments and houses across the country could be the target for the twenty and twenty-five per cent increases in rents.
Other government estimates:
1.	That at least ninety per cent of leased accommodation in the large urban areas is rented on a month-to-month basis. Tenants in this category will be among the first to be hit by the authorized hikes.
2.	Some of this type of accommodation is rented on a weekly and not a monthly basis, and that means that only a week's notice-not a month- need be given by the landlord. If the tenant doesn't pay he can be pushed out the day before Christmas, December 24.
3.	In most cases, however, the rental increases will not go into effect before February 1, 1950. Tenants renting on a monthly basis will have to receive a month's notice as from December 31.
4.	If the government had lifted the controls completely to meet the wishes of Canada's landlords, urban rentals in the big cities would have increased by approximately 100 per cent.

5.	Taking into consideration both rural and urban areas, the new ceilings generally are considered to be about 25 per cent below the level which would prevail if the regulations had been removed completely.
6.	In some areas landlords may not be able to get the tenants to pay the full 20 and 25 per cent hikes. In these areas, such as Kirkland Lake, Ontario, the supply is slightly higher than demand, and it appeared likely that the landlords in these areas "will have to be satisfied with whatever they can get."
The officials emphasized that accommodation constructed since January 1, 1947, does not come under the government's controls, and therefore the increases do not apply. Rentals prices in these cases were beyond the edict of the government's rental administrator. Accommodations in this class are estimated at about 50,000 units. The same thing applies to accommodation vacated on or after November 1, 1948. No estimate was given of the number of units in this category. Tenants with long term leases would not be affected by the rental increases until the leases expire.
That is the end of the statement appearing in the Canadian Press dispatch today and which, as I have said, contains more information than the government has chosen to give the house. I think it leads inescapably to the conclusion that it is high time that the house took this question out of the hands of the government, and put it on a basis where parliament will be making the decisions, where parliament will assert its right to full consultation and to obtain all the information that is available and is required to make a proper decision on the question, and where we will not be compelled simply to accept a fait accompli delivered to us by the government.
Representations have been made to the government by responsible bodies such as the Canadian Legion, which put forward a very strong submission, which apparently has been completely ignored by the government in the decision it has made. Organizations which are close to the problem, such as the federation of mayors and municipalities, and other organizations which have made a firsthand study of the matter, have also made representations, but apparently they have received little or no consideration.
There were rumours going around the house last Thursday afternoon that an announcement was to be made that evening in regard to increases in controlled rents. Rumour had it that the increase might be 10 per cent, or in some cases 15 per cent. I venture to say there is not a member of the house, apart from members of the government, who dreamed for a moment that increases would be allowed to the extent of such figures as 20 and 25 per cent. It would be interesting if the supporters of the government were to come forward and offer their views specifically on the percentages of increase which the government has decided

upon. Let us hear from some of the members of the house who support the government, who were very eloquent on this subject during the election campaign, and who said, for instance, that they were going to uphold rent control.
As a matter of fact, there is one hon. member of the house, a colleague of mine from the city of Toronto, who interested himself in this subject to the point where he wanted to give assistance to the government in a reference pending before the Ontario courts regarding the constitutionality of federal rent control. On October 20 he wrote a letter to every hon. member of the house pointing out that the lawsuit was coming up, and that the federal government was to be represented by counsel. He went on to say:
It has occurred to me that your constituents may be interested in providing counsel for the government with evidence to assist the court at the trial. I have many constituents who wish to present evidence for consideration of counsel representing the government. Because of this, I shall be pleased to work with you or your constituents as to evidence which your constituents may want to present, all with the view to ensuring a full and proper trial of this case now before the courts.
The letter is signed "Charles Henry, member for Toronto-Rosedale".
I should be interested to know the views of the hon. member for Rosedale on these increases. I should be interested to hear the views of Liberal members from the city of Toronto who when at home in their ridings have not been silent on the subject of the difficulties of housing conditions. We will await with interest their contribution to the discussion, and their specific comments on the increases that have been promulgated by the government.
I mentioned that no one expected that the increases would reach the figures announced of 20 and 25 per cent. One would like to know what relationship these percentages bear to uncontrolled rents, or what the increases might be expected to be if rents were decontrolled. That is one of the things that I think a parliamentary committee, if it had the opportunity to go into the question, would like to know.
The minister has talked on previous occasions-and I think this is the expression he has used-of "cushioning the shock of complete decontrol." If the 25 per cent increase represents a cushioning of the shock, then I think that the tenants of Canada will plead with Providence to spare them any more of these government cushions. On what was the percentage based in each case? How did the government arrive at it? It takes one's mind back to the method, described by an hon. member of the house, by which the
Rent Control
government arrived at the particular percentage of devaluation of the Canadian dollar. He described it as a case of putting some figures in a hat, and then somebody, presumably the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), put his hand in the hat and drew out a figure.

speechtext: That was the Tory policy.

speechtext: If the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) knows where the government got the figures of 20 and 25 per cent, I will be happy to sit down and let him tell the house.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: By using the best of good judgment.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Isn't that informative?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Just as informative as your speech. You have not committed yourself on rent control.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I infer that the hon. member for Halton has given his complete blessing and approval to these percentage increases. He says they represent good judgment. It will remain for other government supporters either to rise and applaud, as has the hon. member for Halton, this government cushioning of the shock by means of these increases, or to say that they have different opinions. It remains for hon. members of the house to say. If they are satisfied with these arbitrary percentages, very well; they may well say so. Certainly their silence, if they do not speak to the contrary, will properly be interpreted in the same way as the words of the hon. member for Halton who has said that these percentages are the result of good judgment. The house, the country at large, and tenants by the hundreds of thousands, are left in a state of continuing uncertainty. It is the tenants particularly who are going to suffer from the uncertainty because they are left in a position where, overnight, the government can announce more increases, and apply more of these measures that they call cushioning the shock.
Now, sir, here are some of the things which I say have not been considered by the government. In the first place the circumstances of the tenants have not been taken into account. There are great numbers of Canadian tenants to whom this measure is not going to be a cushion but a great shock. The government does not seem to be aware of the fact, as members of parliament should be aware from their personal relations with their constituents, that many Canadian tenants are just holding their heads above

Rent Control
water today, with limited incomes and the high cost of living. This is one reason why from now on parliament should take over from the government responsibility in regard to this matter, and make laws to meet the need. Now, with an increase by such a large percentage, it simply means that great numbers of tenants are not going to be able to pay these rents. I am sure I do not need to quote figures in regard to the increase in the cost of living. As of October 1 that figure had reached 162-2, (1935-1939 = 100) and now the government decrees another substantial increase which will seriously affect those families whose economic affairs are in such delicate balance today. I do not think it was much of a contribution toward easing the fears of such people for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to make the announcement he made in Montreal on November 6, where he is quoted in a Canadian Press dispatch as follows:
He expressed the opinion further wage demands would not be justified-"it must be understood that in recent years wage rates have gone up very much higher than rental costs."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And that is true.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The minister must be aware that already notice has been served by some labour organizations that increases in wages are going to be demanded in the light of these increased rentals.
On the other hand, and I want to emphasize this, the order is simply flat and arbitrary in its application, and does not take account of the fact that today many people who are occupying quite comfortable and in fact luxurious housing accommodation can well afford to pay uncontrolled rents. I have never been able to understand why wealthy people who choose to live in luxurious apartments or to rent luxurious homes must be protected by rent control. I wish to see rent control preserved now for the people who need it in order to keep their heads above water. I do not see any need to retain rent control for the benefit of people in comfortable circumstances.
In the next place this order, because it is flat and arbitrary, does not take account of the great variety of conditions existing across Canada. There is the greatest variety; yet this is an arbitrary order that applies right across the country without regard to geographical variations, or variations as between urban and rural municipalities.
In the next place it does not take account of those tenants who are subletting their properties at handsome profits. There is no provision in the order under which the owners may repossess such accommodation.
In the next place the timing of this announcement has been almost incredibly bad. Here we are with winter coming on and

these increases are announced, some of them to take effect before Christmas and others in the middle of the winter. If this was in the mind of the government all along it would have been interesting if they had announced it before the by-elections were held a week or two ago, so the people in those constituencies would have had an opportunity to pass judgment.
In the next place, this order does not take account of any obligation on the part of landlords to repair the premises. There is nothing in this order providing that landlords who increase rents by these large percentages are required to carry out any repairs, which in many cases have been delayed for years.
In the next place the order does not relate itself specifically to the increased costs of the landlords. For instance, on August 22 the minister announced that in the city of Toronto a four per cent increase in rents would be allowed to take care of increased taxes accompanying re-assessment in that city. I should like to know whether in the case of my city the latest increase is in addition to that four per cent, or whether the four per cent is to be swallowed up in the increase of twenty or twenty-five per cent.
In the next place this order makes no attempt at all to deal with the discrimination that still exists in a great number of cases, even in the same locality and the same community. When the deadline was first established in 1941 in connection with rent control, many landlords missed it, and since that time they have not had an adequate opportunity to bring their rents into line with others in close proximity to them. These discriminations are continuing, and are being exaggerated by this flat percentage increase.
In conclusion, sir, in the face of arbitrary actions like these by this government I say it is high time this house stepped into the picture and undertook a review of the situation by a proper committee. We are not going to meet the need by sudden, drastic measures of this kind. In his statement, at page 1434 of Hansard, the minister said:
... it is our policy to permit this adjustment to be made gradually rather than abruptly.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if this is a gradual adjustment I think the people of Canada had better learn how long and to what extent they must continue to be at the mercy of these arbitrary decisions on the part of the government. Let this house make it known to the government now that we want an end to the chaos and confusion caused by these sudden government decisions. Let us undertake in parliament now a proper review of this whole situation and write legislative measures with due regard for the needs of all Canadians, which will meet this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this might be an appropriate time for me to say a few words on this question of rent control and the reasons which prompt the government to announce the measures of decontrol which I announced in the house last Thursday evening.
With respect to the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Cold well), let me say at once that his position and that of his party is thoroughly consistent. As he said quite frankly, they advocated the continuation of all controls after the end of the war, including rental control. The stand they take today is no different from the stand they have taken right through the piece. The position of the Liberal party has been different. Before the election of 1945 we pledged ourselves to a gradual and orderly decontrol policy. In fact rental control is the last of the major wartime controls remaining. The attitude of the Progressive Conservative party is not nearly so consistent. Pretty steadily throughout the life of the last parliament they advocated the abolition of all controls.

Rent Control

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What did you do in the byelections? You did not dare to advocate it then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I was making this statement, Mr. Speaker, as a preface to what I have to say about rental controls as such, and about the circumstances which prompted the government to make this further decontrol move. I believe I hardly need say to the house that the government felt this would be an unpopular move. Nevertheless, it is sometimes necessary, even for governments, to do things which may not be universally popular but which may be the proper things to do. The government came to the conclusion that a modification of the rental control regulations, some eight years after they were first adopted, was a step which should be taken.
I have had a good deal of personal experience with the removal of controls of one sort or another, and I found that the more rigid and more successful the controls have been, the more difficult it is to remove them for reasons which I think will be fully understood by all members. These rental controls were part of a general wartime control program. At that time we controlled salaries, wages, prices; we controlled virtually everything which entered into the cost of living. These controls have now disappeared, leaving rental control as the sole survivor of these major wartime controls.
I think with the possible exception of my friends in the C.C.F. party, all members will agree that the federal government cannot and should not continue in the field of rental control. It does not lie within the field of federal jurisdiction under ordinary circumstances. I may say at this point that counsel for the dominion government will contend before the supreme court, on the reference which I announced the other evening, that the federal government has the right to taper off rent controls in a gradual manner; but they will not contend that we have the right to continue them indefinitely.
What is the history of this decontrol program so far as rentals are concerned? The house will recall that in October of last year, after the government had given a good deal of consideration to the constitutional policy of the dominion to continue in this field, I wrote a letter to all provincial premiers in which I stated that the right of the dominion to do so had been challenged in the courts. I offered to abandon rent control in any province if any provincial government desired to take it over, and offered to make the facilities of the rent control administration available as well as to pay the cost for a year.
I am free to confess it did not surprise me that none of the provinces accepted that

Rent Control
offer. Some of the provinces talk a good deal about provincial autonomy, but when it comes to assuming an unpopular responsibility they are not nearly so ready to talk about it. Be that as it may, none of the provinces saw fit to take on that obligation. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I am not attaching any blame to them for failing so to do; I am merely stating the facts.
The other evening I announced I was writing to the provincial premiers stating that we now intended to refer to the supreme court the question of our right to continue in the rental control field until we taper off the control, and orderly decontrol has been established. I repeat my statement that if any province cares to enter the field and take over the responsibility, the dominion will suspend its rental regulations in that province.
It may well be that the people of some of the provinces would be prepared to see rent control in effect on a permanent or semipermanent basis. If so, they must seek action from their provincial legislatures. We can do nothing about it and we should not mislead the public into thinking that we can. It was for this reason that I offered a year ago to vacate the field to the provinces, and that is why I repeated the same offer last Thursday night. As I say, no province has as yet come forward with a request that the dominion withdraw its rental controls in that province to permit the provincial legislature to assume that responsibility.
So far as the federal government is concerned, it has consistently followed a policy of orderly decontrol. It has proceeded step by step exempting certain classes of dwellings from controls, authorizing rent increases, and gradually returning to the owners the right to gain possession of their own homes. We could, of course, have decided to abandon rent control entirely on March 31 when the present legislation expires. That policy was considered, and seriously considered. We were strongly urged to do that. I do not think I am betraying cabinet secrets when I say that some of my colleagues thought that might be a desirable course to follow. The government decided, after the most careful and prolonged consideration, that it should proceed to relax controls rather than bring them to an end abruptly.
As I said before, the government recognized that an authorized increase in rental ceilings would be unpopular. We also had ample evidence that an abrupt ending of rental control would create a situation of extreme gravity. I am not going to burden the house with details, but I am sure that many of you are familiar with the rents being charged for houses and apartments that are no longer

under control. I have been told that, in many cases and especially in the larger industrial centres, rents have doubled or gone up as much as fifty to seventy-five per cent after the removal of control.
In answer to the question put, I think, by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) or the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I am not sure which, I am told by the rentals administration people who have been studying this question throughout the years that it is impossible to tell what would happen if rental controls were suddenly removed. Our information from rentals officers in the field has convinced the government, however, that a most confused and disorderly situation would arise. Such a course of action should therefore be avoided. Consequently, we decided to take another step toward eventual decontrol.
This was a substantial step, and it was intended to be. In spite of the laughter which greeted my remark a moment ago, it does not mean that all rentals will go up by twenty or twenty-five per cent. My own estimation is, we will see whether it is borne out by events, that in a great many cases the increase will not be that much. In centres where the shortage of rental accommodation is most acute, probably the majority of the landlords will take advantage of the maximum ceiling allowed. My estimate is that it will not be an across-the-board increase. This merely gives tenants and landlords the right to bargain within that range. My opinion, which is supported by the rental authorities, is that there will not be a horizontal increase of either twenty or twenty-five per cent.
Be that as it may, I felt and the government felt that if a base could be fixed we could, through those who have been charged by the government with administering this admittedly difficult and onerous control, control the maximum increase to an over-all margin within which landlords and tenants might bargain.
I repeat that this move in the decontrol of rents was part and parcel of our decontrol program announced prior to the election of 1945; and the increases granted were not based on any estimate of the rise in costs or on the needs of the landlords or of the ability of the tenant to pay. Nevertheless, in view of some of the comments that have been made, I want to place before the house with regard to rentals some facts and figures that do not appear to have been sufficiently emphasized.
According to the dominion bureau of statistics, the rent index on September 1 of this year stood at 123-9. That index is based on the period 1935-39; so that, broadly speaking, there has been an increase of about 24 per cent in rents since pre-war years. I

should point out that this index is based not only on houses that are under the ceiling but also on new dwellings which have never been under control and also on dwellings which for one reason or another have been exempted from the ceiling.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Do the figures include light housekeeping rooms?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I could not answer my hon. friend offhand; but there has been no increase in the rentals of light housekeeping rooms.
I make this point that I have made because it means that, on the average, dwellings which are still under control have risen by even less than the 24 per cent increase shown by the index figure which I have just quoted. Since November, 1941, when the ceiling came into effect, the rent index has been raised by only 12-7 points; that is, from 111-2 to 123-9.
I think it is relevant in the circumstances to look at the figure for prices generally. The cost of living index, which includes rents, of course, has risen by 62-2 per cent since pre-war years as against 24 per cent for rents themselves. It is also relevant, I think, to make a comparison between wages and rents. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, average wage rates in non-agricultural industries and average weekly earnings in manufacturing are both up by over 90 per cent since 1939.
An even more striking comparison is that between November, 1941, when the wartime controls on prices, wages and rents came into effect, and the present time. In November, 1941, the rent index stood at 111-2. Today, as I have said, it stands at 123 -9. The percentage increase in rents therefore is, as I said a moment ago, 12-7 points or 11-4 per cent, which I would repeat includes decontrolled as well as controlled dwellings.
What about prices and wages in the same period-that is, the period since rental controls first came into effect in November, 1941? The cost of living index since November, 1941, has risen from 116-3 to 162-2; that is, by 45 -9 points or 39 per cent. Average wage rates in 1948, which is the latest data available, are up by 73 per cent since 1941, and average weekly earnings by 63 per cent between November, 1941, and the present time.
There is one other point I should like to clarify. In my statement last Thursday night I said:
Landlords will be permitted to offer a term certain lease for not less than one year in consideration of a rental increase of not more than 20 per cent in the case of unheated self-contained dwellings and of not more than 25 per cent in the case of heated self-contained dwellings.
These increases will make a total of general over-all increases permitted since November, 45781-98
Rent Control
1941-a period of eight years-of 30 per cent for unheated accommodation and 40 per cent for heated accommodation. While the present increases of 20 per cent and 25 per cent are in addition to the previous increases of 10 per cent and 15 per cent, the government has never intended to apply the one percentage increase to the other, which would, of course, have resulted in more than an over-all general increase of 30 per cent or 40 per cent. In other words, the increases are not cumulative. The mechanics to be employed by the rentals administration in carrying out this policy are now being worked out and they will appear in the relevant orders.
My hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. party said that this policy represented an entire disregard of the welfare of the majority of the people. I am aware, of course, that there are a great many more tenants than there are owners in the country. But I have never felt that mere numbers justified the perpetuation of unfairness or injustice, assuming that such unfairness or injustice exists.
In another debate yesterday some reference was made to matters of discrimination. In view of the figures which I have given to the house as to the increase in wages, salaries and other items, as compared with rentals, I ask any member who is honest with himself whether he believes that the owner of a property on which he has had his rent frozen since 1941 until the present day or who has had the moderate increase granted up to the present time, is being treated on a comparable basis with regard to other groups in the community. To me, Mr. Speaker, the answer to that question is self-evident.
When one talks about ignoring the welfare of the majority of the people, if one accepts majority rule in matters of this kind, then of course my hon. friend is right. If one accepts the proposition that in matters of fairness and equity one should be governed by the number of heads that you count, then of course my hon. friend is absolutely right, and my friend the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), with his demagogic appeal, is absolutely right. But if you are talking about questions of fairness as between one group of the community and another, then it is perfectly clear that the existing structure of frozen rentals is unfair to the majority of people who are receiving them. It is in an attempt, first, to proceed with its program of orderly decontrol and, second, in an attempt to be fair to a group of Canadians in the community, that the government is putting forward this policy. It believes that it is a sound policy and it intends to back it up.

Rent Control

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I should like to add some thoughts on this subject, Mr. Speaker, before the debate closes. I was greatly interested in the remarks made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the reasons for their decontrol policy and the method which they have outlined. I was particularly interested in noting what the minister had to say about the Progressive Conservative party and their attitude toward rental control, although I hold no brief for the Progressive Conservative party. The minister said that the Progressive Conservative party should have made their stand known to the public before the general election. At the time he made that statement I was wondering if there was any party in the house which was less considerate of public opinion in this regard than was the Liberal government; for certainly had the public of Canada been acquainted with the so-called decontrol methods of the government, as put forth now, they would have shown their position in no uncertain manner. But they were not permitted that opportunity. It was thought wise by the government-and politically it was probably good judgment-to save this rent policy until after the general election.
My mind goes back to other things which the public should have been informed upon before the general election. Had this rent control policy, along with the flour-milling report, been presented to the people of Canada before the general election, I am sure that the Liberal government would have found that the people of Canada were dissatisfied with some of the operations of this government.
In speaking of the stand that parties have taken with regard to decontrol, let me say that the Social Credit party has always taken the view that we should have controls where necessary, and on no other occasion. But this is not one of the times when controls on rent should be lifted, or indeed lifted to the extent that they have been under the new rent control order.
In regard to this subject the premier of Alberta said the other day that he believed in decontrol in normal times, but these are decidedly not normal times. The minister speaks about having a proper decontrol method, a decontrol method which would be less severe on the majority of people. He said that they have tried in their decontrol policy to cushion the shock. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether that is exactly true. Under the decontrol methods used by the government it seems to me that there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction, discontent and hardship. I want to point out instances of this hardship and discontent. Today there are a great many people whose incomes will not

warrant an increase in rent. Several organizations throughout the country have estimated that a man cannot pay more than 20 per cent, or one-fifth of his income, in rent. In Calgary not so long ago one large concern, not a provincial industry but a national one, was paying its employees $100 to $115 a month. If a man is receiving $100 to $115 a month how in the world can he stand an increase of twenty to twenty-five per cent? I know of some of these men who were paying $45 a month in rent. If you add an increase of twenty-five per cent on that, and it has to be paid out of an income of $100 or $115 a month, it can readily be seen that there is room for complaint and that there is decided hardship in these cases.
The minister may say, "Oh, a great many of these landlords will not take advantage of this increase." I think that is true. But can you leave such a major problem as this open to the possibility that some landlords will not take advantage of the increase? Probably the landlords who are already charging $140 to $150 a month for rent will not take advantage of it and increase their rates by twenty to twenty-five per cent; but there are a great many landlords who are charging $40 to $45 a month. These landlords who are dealing with people on a very moderate income will take advantage of this decontrol order. They will raise their rents to the people who can least afford it.
It has been stated, and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed it out a while ago, that about four million people will be affected by this so-called decontrol of rent and over 50,000 housing accommodation units will be affected. There are a great many inequitable cases. Let me give the house some of them. New houses that were built prior to November 1, 1948-it used to be 1947, but this order carries it through to 1948-are entirely free from rent control. Then certain houses are vacated for some reason or other. They are free of rent control. Suppose a tenant decides to move out for some reason or other. That house immediately becomes free of rent control. There is another house of equal value in the same residential part of the city in which the tenant still remains. In one case the rent is frozen and in the other it is free. Show me what justice there is in a situation such as that. There are two houses of equal value in the same part of the city. The owner of one is absolutely free to charge any rent that he can get. I know some men who are charging $150 to $200 a month. The house right next to it is under control. There is just no equality in that. Surely this government could arrange a decontrol policy under

which these unfair and inequitable conditions could be ironed out and a logical and decent decontrol policy put into effect.
There is no question about it, Mr. Speaker, that the action of the government at this time in raising the rents from twenty to twenty-five per cent will greatly affect those people who can least afford to pay any increase. Right off the bat I am going to agree with the minister that there are some instances where landlords need an adjustment in their rents. I pointed that out a few moments ago. But there are many instances where there is unfairness, and where there is no attempt to make a uniform policy in regard to these rents, and consequently a great deal of hardship will be felt throughout the country. How can people on these low incomes survive if their cost of living is going to be jumped twenty to twenty-five per cent on one item alone? It just is not reasonable to expect them to be able to survive. The people are entitled to some reasoning in the decontrolling of rents.
Let me give you one illustration, Mr. Speaker, to show that people cannot afford an increase in rent. Take old age pensioners, for instance. How are old age pensioners going to be able to pay an increase in rent? I do not care how small the increase may be. At this point I may say that it may be necessary for the government to subsidize some landlords, but in regard to the old age pensioners there is no justification for allowing an increase in rent. They just cannot pay it. All of the people on fixed incomes are going to be materially affected, and most of them are going to be unable to make any financial adjustments in this field.
The minister speaks about the government's policy of decontrol. He went so far as to say that it was questionable whether the legal position of the government was sound in continuing rent control. I can only say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the premier of Quebec was right when he said the other day, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen:
Government Action "Remarkable"-Duplessis
Premier Duplessis yesterday described as "remarkable" announcement of the federal government's intention to obtain a supreme court decision on the validity of rent controls.
"Nine years after the federal government passed a law, they want to find out if they had a right to enact it," he said at a press conference.
"It seems remarkable. It reminds me of stories about an ancient Scottish practice of hanging a man and afterward holding a trial to see if he is guilty."
That is just about the position in which the federal government finds itself now. Did they not know that their legal position might not have been any too sound prior to June 27? I think they would have known it then.

Rent Control
Why did they not come out frankly and tell the people the intentions they had, the practices they were going to put into force right after the election? They were not much concerned about dealing fairly with the public at that time; in fact, I think it was just about the opposite.
Let me quote briefly from the Ottawa-Journal of Monday, November 7, under the heading "Mr. Abbott Set With Long Lease But Colleagues Face Rent Hoists", just to show how utterly impossible it is going to be for people to pay the rents they are likely to be asked. It states:
An official cited the following as- an example for a heated self-contained dwelling if all relaxations were transformed into increased rent:
Basic rent, 1947, $100 monthly.
Ten per cent increase allowed April, 1947, making rent $110.
Five per cent increase allowed for heated dwelling, October, 1948, making rent $115.50.
Twenty-five per cent increase allowed September 15, 1949, making rent $144.37.
Mr. Abbott and his officials told the Journal it was obvious that if rent controls were eliminated completely a chaotic situation would arise. They have had experience of rents being as much as doubled on houses free of rent controls because they were built since 1947 or had been released because the occupants under rent control had moved away. These experiences indicated that without control rents would skip sky-high in many cases.
That shows how rents can increase. There will be cases where it will be utterly impossible for the people of Canada to meet these conditions.
A moment ago I spoke about the increased cost of living. It has been indicated by the trade unions that they are going to demand increases in wages. The ones to whom I referred a short time ago, who are receiving $100 or $115 a month, are not under the large trade unions, and therefore they will not receive the benefits of trade union activities and protection to get increases in wages.
In the same article from which I quoted a moment ago we find this paragraph:
Trades and labour congress unions are considering asking for higher wages as a result of the government's rent boost action, TLC President Percy Bengough said today.
There is no question about it that the action the government has taken upon itself to increase rents by 20 and 25 per cent is going to start another surge across the country for increased wages. We cannot blame the trade unions for asking increases in their wage scales when the government makes it absolutely impossible for wage earners to carry on at present wage rates. The government is creating this chaotic state. They are demanding that unions go out on strike in an endeavour to obtain increased wages. The government is creating the condition which is

Rent Control
throwing thousands of people out of employment through the necessity of having to go on strike to obtain increased wages resulting from government action.
This is not the time when rent controls should be increased to the extent of 20 per cent. It is not the time to increase rents-a time when old age pensioners and others, on fixed incomes cannot be expected to pay such rents. Surely it is not the time to increase rents by 20 and 25 per cent when the great majority of our working people are earning from $100 to $150 a month.
I could take hon. members to Calgary and show them hundreds upon hundreds of people, married men with families, who are living on $35 a week. They cannot afford these increased rentals. No matter what the minister may say with respect to some landlords who will not take full advantage of the increase, I venture to say that at least 75 per cent of them will take advantage of it to some extent, and raise their rents. Those increases will fall most heavily upon the people who can least afford it.
For that reason and for others which I have given, I am definitely of the opinion that this is not the time for the government so to increase rents.

I am in favour of having rent controls continued. I do not want the controls taken off until housing conditions are improved.

speechtext: They are still on.

speechtext:
Only technically. A majority of the members from Montreal, with the exception of the Minister of Finance himself, seem to be in favour of rent control. I think there is room to argue that the residue of rent controls remaining is not, from a practical view, control at all.
I hope therefore that before the debate is concluded we may hear from some of the Liberal backbenchers. I hope they will not have been frightened by what the minister said today. I would hope, too, that when the Montreal members speak, they will speak as they did to the reporter last week. What is more, I hope after they have spoken in that manner, they will vote as they have talked- and not do as one Liberal member did yesterday, speak one way, and vote the other.
The reaction to these whopping rental increases across Canada can be described only as one of profound shock. In effect many landlords are going to be able to raise their rents from 20 to 25 per cent. The manner in which the minister introduced these rental increases last Thursday night is an affront to the authority of this parliament. As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has said, the Minister of Finance presented us with a fait accompli. Members were given no opportunity to debate this basic issue. Even some of the Liberal backbenchers were shocked by the announcement. That is, they were shocked if we can believe what we read in the Ottawa Citizen, this morning.
I quote:
Several rank-and-file Liberal members of parliament plan to ask the government to reconsider its announced Intention of allowing 20 to 25 per cent boosts in domestic rental ceilings.
A number of members are claiming the announced increases in rental ceilings came "as a complete surprise." They claim they had no idea before the announcement was made the increases would be as substantial as they were.
I do not blame my Liberal friends for being pretty peeved. Has parliament lost its right, Mr. Speaker, to even discuss a basic issue? Have we lost our right to debate

a problem before a decision is announced? I am beginning to wonder if we have been sent down here-and I include Liberal members-simply to rubber-stamp decisions which the cabinet has already made. I hope that is not true, but if it is I want to say that there might be some danger in the future of our becoming as ineffective as the German Reichstag once was under Adolf Hitler. The way in which the cabinet has appeared to run things recently seems to me to be similar to the way the Cominform runs the Czechoslovakian government-by decree.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Isn't that ridiculous.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Hon. members will not forget that the minister made his announcement last Thursday evening with only about five minutes left before the house adjourned. We did not even have time to ask questions let alone to debate the issue. Nor will hon. members forget either, that the minister who flouted the authority of parliament Thursday evening is the same minister who, a year and a half ago, introduced taxation by radio to Canada. As I understand these rental changes, they do not become effective until December 15.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: High class debate.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Why should not parliament have had the opportunity to debate the changes before they were actually introduced? Why were rent controls originally introduced? They were brought into being eight or nine years ago to prevent property owners, in face of the acute housing shortage, from taking undue advantage of the situation to charge excessive rents. In other words, they were introduced to help to keep the cost of living down to a reasonable figure. I will say at once that in my opinion rental control helped to do that but if rental control was desirable in 1941 why is it not desirable in 1949? Today the housing situation is infinitely worse than it was eight years ago. We can take the words of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) as proof of that fact because he said at page 118 of Hansard:
New housing, even at the present record rate of production, is barely keeping up with current needs and making no important inroads into the backlog.
In the past eight or nine years our population has increased substantially, and as a consequence housing is in short supply. Landlords are in a better position today to charge unfair rent than they were in 1941. In my opinion the increases which the minister announced last Thursday night were so sharp that we can well question whether the residue of controls is of any practical value. The new regulations will render millions of
Rent Control
Canadians vulnerable to the housing shortage and to the whims of their landlords. In many cases the last rental increases will mean a total increase of as much as 45 per cent since the first unfreezing order two years ago. Many Canadian tenants are going to be caught in the squeeze between higher rentals and the shortage of housing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) admitted that much over the week end.

speechtext: Over the week end the minister had a good many interviews-some of them rather unhappy. According to one reporter, the minister said he was sure that landlords would not take advantage of the full amount of increase allowed, but that they would be "kindly". I am sure some landlords will be reasonable and will not take all they can get, but I am equally sure there are many other landlords who will take every cent they can get, and who will not be kindly. I think the minister's admonition to some of these individuals will be about as effective as pleading with a weasel in a henhouse to be kindly.
