speechtext:
Don't get excited.

Rent Control

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In his speech last Thursday night the Minister of Finance made some very pious statements. I have heard a good many of his pious statements in the last few years, but I am beginning to take them with a grain of salt. At page 1433 of Hansard he said:
The government intends to continue with its program of orderly decontrol as rapidly as conditions warrant . . .
Further on he said:
We believe that gradual and orderly decontrol is the right policy.
Further on again he said:
, , . it is our policy to permit this adjustment to be made gradually rather than abruptly.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Don't you agree with that?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: As he does so often, the minister talked one way and acted another, because as soon as he had said that the government believed in orderly decontrol, he announced drastic rental increases of 20 and 25 per cent. Where is there any consistency in that kind of action? I admit at once that there are cases of individual hardship so far as some landlords are concerned, and I think it is fair and reasonable, if that type of hardship exists, that those landlords should have been given some increase; but why give an increase right across the board regardless of whether or not there is hardship, and regardless of the type of property?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Rough justice.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Surely if rental increases were needed at this time, surely if the minister was genuinely sincere in his statement that he wanted orderly decontrol, an increase of perhaps 5 per cent would have sufficed at this time. When rental control was introduced in 1941 the cost of living index stood at 111*7. Today the cost of living index is 162-2, an increase of almost .47 per cent. I say that Canadians are far more vulnerable today to rental increases than they would have been in 1941. Rental increases can only mean one thing. They will almost certainly mean that the cost of living index will reach an all-time high. That in turn will probably mean a new series of wage demands from the various unions which cannot help but have an inflationary effect. Many union leaders have already warned us of that fact. G. Russell Harvey, national organizer of the American Federation of Labor, had this to say on Saturday in Montreal:
It is going to provide a dislocation of what was otherwise becoming a stabilized wage condition. Now, it has become necessary for labour to demand higher wages to meet the added cost of living forced by the increases in rents.

I believe that the government of Canada once again has sacrificed the obvious wellbeing of the majority of our citizens to a privileged group, this time the property owners. It is quite true that the minister is getting rid of a political headache, but by prematurely scrapping rental controls the government is indirectly causing extreme hardship, and unnecessarily so, to a great many people of Canada. Trade unions, consumer organizations, veteran groups and many other groups have been protesting. The views of one of the officers of the Canadian Legion are to be found in the Toronto Star of November 5 in an article reading as follows;
Norman Gillespie, chairman of the housing committee of the Quebec command of the Canadian Legion, said the government, in allowing the increases, had broken faith with Canadian fighting men who died to make it possible for landlords to retain their properties. "Instead of families being protected, they are being exploited," he said.
May I say that the C.C.F. group dislikes controls as much as any other party in the house. We dislike controls for the sake of control. If there were adequate housing in Canada, and if there were any other way of keeping rents down, we would be quite happy to see rentals decontrolled; but that is not the case.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Is it not true that Saskatchewan or any other province can take over rent control, if it wishes?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I am coming to that in a moment; I have a major point I want to make, but I thank the hon. member for his question.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You will never get to it.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I shall get there in a minute. In the minister's statement there was one significant sentence at page 1433 of Hansard:
The government has therefore decided to refer the question of the validity of the rental regulations to the supreme court . . .
This means that nine years after the law was passed, nine years during which the government has been enforcing it, the minister suddenly decides to go to the courts to see whether or not it is valid. As Shakespeare might have said: There is something rotten in the state-not Denmark this time, but in Canada. Personally I believe this government is trying to get rid of its responsibility for maintaining rental controls in exactly the same way it dealt with the margarine issue. It is going to do everything in its power to have the supreme court throw out all rental controls, as far as the federal government is concerned. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has had the reputation in many parts of Canada of being the extreme right winger

of the Liberal government. Perhaps he is proud of that reputation; I do not know. I want to tell him, however, that after his performance in the last few days, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is becoming a first-rate challenger for that very dubious honour.
I say the government betrayed the confidence of the electors of Canada, who supported them so strongly in the last election, in abandoning rent control; and I believe the government is shirking its responsibility in a very cold, very calculating way. Today the ten provincial governments are the last line of defence, one might say, to protect tenants from landlords who may wish to raise rents too high. Let us hope these provincial governments will act with a great deal more courage than has been shown by the Minister of Finance. I am happy to know that in Saskatchewan we have stand-by legislation. I believe ours is the only provincial government having legislation of that kind, and I am reasonably sure that our provincial government will retain rental controls there.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this matter, inasmuch as our city is very much interested in it. I do not intend to criticize what the government has done, or what anyone has done. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who moved the motion, referred to something I had forgotten about, a motion in connection with a national housing and reconstruction policy which I moved on February 17, 1936. The subheading reads:
Proposed measures in respect of housing, land settlement, reforestation:	youth in education,
industry and employment.
The motion was in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, Canada should immediately adopt a comprehensive national housing, building, reconstruction, renovation, slum clearance, land settlement and reforestation policy adapted to its circumstances. . . .
In that connection I suggested that a committee should be appointed. This motion was moved in 1936, when conditions throughout the world were bad. People were out of work; large numbers of our youths were riding the rods; thousands of my constituents were on relief; skilled workers, carpenters, bricklayers, lathers, plasterers, men who had never known what it was to be without employment, were walking the streets. In the riding I represented at that time sixty-five per cent of the people owned their own homes, but because of the intolerable conditions which obtained many lost their properties. As I said at that time, the wealth of this country does not consist only of the natural resources of the sea, of the soil, of the forest, of the mine or of the lakes; it does
Rent Control
not consist only of the grain in our great elevators or the shipping in our harbours. There is a more glorious treasure than that. It is the character of our people. This character, through unemployment and the lack of housing, has been gradually destroyed. The care of our young citizens is our most important duty. Several billion dollars have been spent on the construction of railways but only a few million have been spent on housing. Our school boards are doing the best they can, but they are having a hard time of it.
As I said, at that time we were in difficulty because of world conditions. Now we must realize that the housing question is very closely associated with public health. Unless you have proper housing you cannot have a healthy rising generation. What did they do over in the mother country, which has been criticized so much in late years? They led the whole civilized world at that time. Our former sovereign, King Edward VIII, was one of the pioneers in this connection. He visited the slums of London and Wales, and travelled all over Britain. In 1937 he awakened the whole country to the necessity of correcting the slum problem. What was the result of his campaign? Two million new homes were constructed under the auspices of various public and private bodies.
We have to look at the cause and effect of this whole problem. Canada was once a nation of property owners. Practically every man owned a property of some sort, but that is not the situation today. I have no doubt tha-our own city does more to provide for our city suburbs sewers, water service, roads, health services, cheap light and power and efficient transportation than any other city in Canada. As I say, in the old days practically everyone owned some property; a small farm, a market garden, a grocery store, a mill or something of the kind. We were all property owners, some small, some moderate, and some large; but this condition gradually changed. What caused that change? Canadians owned real estate; and that individual ownership, on the comparatively extensive scale on which it then existed, was the basis of Canada's national life. But the politics of big business has practically destroyed pastoral Canada, and it is the duty of parliament, the duty of members of all parties, to take this into consideration. We must dedicate our efforts to a solution to this problem of housing, and one of the most effective means of bringing that about is to restore the condition that existed when most people owned a little property, as in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and Whitney in Ontario.
15S0

Rent Control
Then Canada was indeed the land of the free; Canada was the home of artisans and farmers; Canada was a democratic country.
In nothing is the determined spirit of the mother country more evident than in her program of construction of new homes. People who have been in England in the past two or three years have returned to Canada enraptured with what they saw over there in the construction of new houses; the spirit of the mother country has been particularly evident in what she has done in that direction. Large apartment houses are going up all over the countryside. Houses have been built by government subsidy, and England has shown her determination properly to house as large a proportion as possible of the poorer classes of the population. One man remarked to me that low-cost housing there had ceased to be a political issue, and I submit that the same should be true in this country. Low-cost housing is a permanent government policy in England; long may it continue. And it should be here as well. There is great need for construction of houses, not only urban but suburban and rural as well, the last mentioned being the most needed of all. Let me quote something I came across in the reading room the other day. This newspaper item is typical of many; it refers to Windsor:
Today is moving day in the historic and picturesque village of Coinbrook, on the Bath road, near Slough.
That is something that was done in England in the olden days.
Now, I shall conclude what I have to say in a few moments because there are several other members who wish to speak. So far as I can see, this country needs a housing program now.
As I say, this question has been related to public health. In last Sunday's Montreal Standard, I noticed that the fourteen members from the Montreal district stated a policy for Montreal island. If hon. members were consulted, I believe they would say the same thing, that is that a control system with some variations should be continued until the supply of houses is sufficient. Small prefabricated houses should be built. I remember that Mr. Churchill was responsible for the building of about 500,000 of those prefabricated houses in England during 1945 or 1946. The materials were secured in Canada. What have we been doing in this country? We have been doing very little.
I believe that the notice given by the government is too short. Nearly four million tenants will be affected by the new regulations which have been announced. I do not think the policy of the government commends itself to the country. There is no use in the

government kicking the football over here because, as astute politicians, we would kick it right back to them. The government of the day is responsible for a proper housing policy, a proper reconstruction policy and a proper slum clearance policy. It is not for the opposition to do that. The opposition does not seek any political advantage from it.
As has been said in this debate, we gave the government fair warning of what would happen in 1936 or nearly 14 years ago. The policy of the government now is to pass the matter over and to criticize the provinces. If it had not been for the fine autumn weather, which was a blessing to the people of this country, people would have suffered severely from the lack of housing. It was very fortunate that all fall we had fair weather and it looks like the hand of Providence. I believe the first duty of a government is to look after the health, wealth, peace, happiness, prosperity and housing of its people. It should be a national program. One of the mistakes we made at confederation was that some of these matters were not transferred to federal jurisdiction. I believe that housing is really a national problem today.
In connection with my own city, I believe that nothing has contributed to the lack of housing as much as the lack within the city of cheap land. There is no cheap land in the city. I can tell you that land is now about $65 per foot, what little there is left of it in the city. The member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) may remember the time we built a civic carline on the Danforth from Broadview avenue to the east end. It was necessary to acquire from the north side from the township of York all the land for about two hundred and twenty feet on the north side of the street in order to widen the street. It cost little or no money to build that carline. Another streetcar line was the one on Gerrard street. The land was secured for $6 per foot, and that was true even down in the Greenwood riding. Six tickets for ten cents was the rate in those days.
The working people were encouraged by that car service, by the cheap tickets, by the cheap light and by the municipal services. Those services were extended away out into the county, into York township. Suppose this chamber were the city proper. There is the lake and the bay to the south. We extended these services to the east of the city proper, out into the county of York and away to the north beyond the city limits. All the people in this locality were given the same privileges, cheap light, sewers, water, and police protection. There were lots of good roads. I remember when we could not get milk into our city. We had to establish the first good roads in Canada,

which extended for a radius of fifteen miles from the city. So, I say the government should not be so quick in turning this back to the provinces.
I do not believe the notice is any good; it is too short. The provinces should have been consulted before any move was made. I believe the members from the city of Toronto are of the same opinion as the Montreal members. Until such time as the supply of houses is sufficient, new regulations for rent control should not be passed. I may say that if the city of Toronto had a suburban service like Montreal, it could solve its own housing problem. There is no land in the city except at $65 per foot. Then there is the matter of these people being turned out of their houses. There are about four million tenants who are in fear of this in Canada.
What is more necessary than a house? If a person has not a home, he has not anything. The lack of a home interferes with family life and causes many other evils such as delinquency. Just look at the front page of the Ottawa Citizen today. According to it, four million tenants are to be evicted before Christmas. One of the Ottawa judges blames the lack of housing for crime in this city. I believe that something should be done to construct, as early as possible, half a million of these prefabricated small houses such as those that were constructed at Three Rivers, Oshawa and many other places.
Without a steam suburban service I believe that we can make little headway even if the program of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is adopted. Certainly with no cheap land in the city, and without a steam suburban service, there is no chance of our solving the housing program out in the county of York, and we need not look for any scheme to do it. Without transportation and the civic services, the new housing plans will not be worth anything.
In conclusion I want to say this. Many people have been burned to death in the ramshackle buildings that are being used. I have seen houses, occupied by soldiers who served in the second war, in which the windows had to be shut because of smoke; some of these houses are not fit for human habitation, in my opinion. A couple of people were burned in a fire on Church street. I notice that in a fire in the maritimes, five were burned last week end. Fires occur in these old condemned buildings which are not fit for human habitation, and many people have been burned.
As I say, I believe we should have some proper system. This housing problem follows every great war. The Addington administration had it; the two Pitts had it. The question of control and decontrol is one 45781-99
Rent Control
which should not be so suddenly turned over to the provinces. The number of eviction orders which the senior county court judge of the county of York has had runs into the thousands. I believe that something should be done along the lines I suggest.
As to the new way of doing this business, turning it over so suddenly, and passing a new order in council, is all wrong. I believe we should continue some controls. No doubt some soldiers should be allowed to get into their own homes. I believe there should be some variation in order to enable them to do that. People who fought for their country should have some relief accordingly. But I say that the time is too short for the government to take this action at the start of this winter, that the order is too hasty and that it is going to lead to untold hardships during the coming winter. I have in my hand a picture which shows 47 people in Montreal living on top of an old fire station, a place which is unfit for human habitation.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the housing problem is surely one of the major issues stirring up public opinion at the present time. The housing shortage is all the more surprising in that it affects a country that prides itself, and rightly so, on its high industrial potential. There is a shortage throughout the country as a whole but for a long time it has been growing steadily worse in the larger cities. For a long time the situation has reached the critical stage and threatens to lead to consequences whose effects can hardly be foreseen or even exaggerated. This over-all breakdown of the housing industry seems the more irritating in that it affects a country that is privileged in the matter of space and raw materials, such as iron, lumber, etc., in a country where manpower, both plentiful and skilled, is already haunted in certain districts by the spectre of unemployment. Indeed, in some Canadian cities, the housing shortage is almost as acute as in some European countries, where density of population reaches 7,500 people per square mile, as in Belgium, or as in countries devastated by two world wars, in 1914 and in 1939.
Travellers returning from Europe all marvel at the way in which countries so badly damaged by bombing during the last war have managed to rebuild, under particularly difficult circumstances. It may be said, due allowances being made, that the housing situation in Belgium and in Europe is better than here in Canada. Great Britain, France and other countries stand as shining examples that should inspire our own government's policy in this connection.

Rent Control
It is not difficult to understand the reasons for those countries' desperate attempts to solve their housing problem. Housing is among the first concerns of any civilization. It may be said that material civilization consists in properly solving the threefold problem of food, clothing and shelter!
Is it not heart-breaking that our workers are still anxiously wondering where they will find a dwelling, and pay the rent at the end of each month?
I suggest that the matter has not been carefully considered by this government and was settled in a hasty, easy and haphazard way. No constructive, practical and final solution to this knotty problem was evolved by those who had undertaken to consider it. Did peace dry up the source of the energy we displayed throughout the war? How can such a great gap in the domestic economy of our national policy be explained and justified? Are war conditions the indispensable incentives to the vast building projects of which we gave so many examples for the benefit of our allies in Europe during the six years of the last war?
Yet this housing situation has been a feature of our policy many years before the war. This government itself has seen the premonitory signs of the ill we are now deploring. Has it taken any action with a view to preventing the threatening housing shortage? With the coming of war the government has enacted protective measures for the benefit of tenants, who form an overwhelming majority of the population. All citizens have welcomed such a manifestation of elementary prudence on its part during the war years. However, everyone was expecting a solution to this emergency; none has been forthcoming, and we are still awaiting one. The visionless, listless and neglectful policy of the government is responsible for that. To govern is to foresee. The government should have foreseen this emergency and devised means to meet it. It has seen the people accept with heroic patience rationing, as well as the restrictive and repressive measures of the sad period of the European tragedy. It has taken for granted that the patience of the victims of that period of sacrifices would last forever; it has relied on that to postpone the solving of the serious problem which is involved in providing housing for the middle and the working classes in Canada. The war is over. Victory is still floating in the folds of the future Canadian flag. Apparently we are in a period of full prosperity. How can 
we believe those Liberal prophets when hundreds of Canadian family heads are wondering if they will have tomorrow a lodging for their wives and children? Nothing can justify this uninterrupted standstill in the building industry. The sons of the most humble families are apprehensive; their eyes are troubled by the vision of furniture on the sidewalks. Yet they have contributed in no small measure to the victory of our armies. Many are proud to wear military medals which bear testimony to their gallantry. Still they are not sure that tomorrow they shall still have a home, a place to rest after their daily toil.
What miracle, what prodigy is the government awaiting before setting itself into action to find an efficient solution, an adequate remedy to the present crisis which has already lasted too long and worsens daily? The country was prosperous in wartime. The government did not hesitate to spend billions in order to build destructive weapons for our European allies. We rejoice that the sacrifices made by the Canadian people have brought timely relief to those unjustly oppressed populations who, alas, foresee once more the bloody spectre of a new, perhaps remote but more murderous adventure. But we are now living in time of peace. Our natural resources are still there, awaiting peaceful mobilization in favour of our closest allies, the Canadian population. Productively, our manpower is still strong. It is time to capitalize on the financial possibilities of a huge country whose government should be concerned chiefly with the housing of all its citizens.
Far from introducing encouraging and beneficial measures, the Minister of Finance has just taken the tenants by surprise in announcing very drastically a disappointing and substantial raise of 20 and 25 per cent in the present rental rates. The government have always been praised for their insinuating policy, for proceeding by stages before enacting. The undercover processes resorted to during the war had only confirmed this subtle and disturbing diplomacy.	The
sudden announcement by the Minister of Finance has left all our population worried, especially the tenants, who are nonplussed and distressed before a fact brought to them in such a sudden and disappointing manner. Why was that important announcement not made before the election or during the electoral campaign? Was it for fear of disastrous results at the polls?

1SS3
Were landlords right in hoping, prior to the elections, that a few months after June 27 they would be able to obtain a generous increase in rents? It would surely be interesting to know the answers to all these questions. At any rate, the time has come to take heed of the legitimate requests of tenants. The government should avail itself of all the means at its disposal to end that lamentable and ridiculous situation in a country where there is no reason for such an internal calamity. It is praiseworthy to help the various nations of the world in times of emergency, but in peacetime it is the duty of the government to achieve prosperity for its citizens. A country cannot be prosperous as long as its workers are threatened with being thrown out in the street on the very eve of a hard winter. An increase such as the one which the Minister of Finance has just inflicted on tenants will not solve the problem. I therefore urge, on behalf not only of my constituency but of the low-income group, that is to say of tenants all over the country, immediate settlement of this intolerable condition.
Every conflict has found us ready to struggle, to co-operate, even at the cost of billions of dollars. Let the government now show the same concern, the same spirit of self-sacrifice-I ought to say a keener sense of justice and a greater interest in social security-so that our country may break this humiliating deadlock brought about by its internal policy.
Policies such as the Quebec farm loan should make the government aware of the goodwill and solvency of our country's little people; they appreciate the confidence and benefits bestowed upon them by public authorities.
No one can be unaware of the seriousness of the situation in which hundreds of thousands of householders find themselves. Their modest budgets will not allow them, no matter how hard they try, to meet the landlord's new demands. That capitalism will again lose a few feathers, soon to be picked up by the evil-boding bird of communism, is easily foreseen.
The government's decision to refer the rentals control act to the supreme court is not likely to allay a natural concern. This action can do nothing to help the tenant pay his rent. This astute legal device will only add to the irritation of the victims of the coming increase.
Who is it that has been legislating in this field for nine years? Who is it that has brought us to our present difficulties? Who is it that has steered the ship of Canada for 45781-99j
Rent Control
nine years, heedless of the recriminations and protests of all and sundry? It is this govern-' ment. They have no right to throw the helve after the hatchet in this matter of housing and to shift their responsibilities upon others. It is up to the present government to continue its task, as long as this acute shortage prevails, of bridging this gap for which it is responsible. It must find the means whereby a quick and satisfactory solution will be brought to the problem of exorbitant rentals and shortage of housing in this country! The present government has just taken an antisocial and anti-family stand which has created grave unrest among the working classes.
If the present administration uses its accidental and absolute majority to impose dilatory and vexatious measures, it will only succeed in further upsetting the lack of balance of our economic machinery. It is not normal that the government should hesitate in these days of peace and prosperity -a prosperity which has been extolled from every meeting hall-to treat with fairness the people of this country who, for too long now, have been worried and uncertain about the future.
The people do not want any special privilege but only claim for themselves an unequivocal and vital right, from the governments which are entrusted with their economic well-being. If every family cannot be suitably housed at a decent price whom shall the present administration convince that prosperity has been brought to this country by five years of peace after victory?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to place myself on record as protesting, in the name of the population in my riding, against the new rental increases as announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last Thursday. It is a measure which will bring hardship to the majority of Canadians, and which has taken everyone by surprise. To date we have yet to be given some reason for the move. Nowhere have we seen proof that such a tremendous increase was necessary.
On the contrary, rentals have always been one of the major factors in the high cost of living. That is why it is so regrettable that the government has permitted an increase which will heavily load the budgets of the majority of Canadian families. Even before these latest increases many families have had to cut into their food budgets to pay

Prairie Transmission Lines their rent. The situation would be different if they could move to other homes offering rentals in accordance with their means. However at this time, five years after the war, the housing situation is so far from being solved that such a means must be disregarded completely.
I believe the government has shown a complete disregard for the welfare of the ordinary Canadian citizen. Everywhere since last Thursday, from all across Canada, and especially from Quebec and the island of Montreal, these new increases have brought discouraged protests from our people. In my own riding more than 75 per cent of the population is going to be hit by this Christmas present from the Liberal government.
Before taking my seat I should like to ask the minister for the last time to reconsider his decision. Our population really deserves better treatment.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benidickson for the second reading of Bill No. 119, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other evening I addressed the house for a few minutes on the principle of the measure now under consideration and that involved in Bill No. 66, to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company. Tonight we are dealing with Bill No. 119, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. I want to apologize to the hon. member, who is the sponsor of the bill now under discussion, for not having a eopy of it at the time. As I see it, the principle of this bill, and that of the bill to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company, are the same. Shall we part with any more of our natural resources? I have always taken the position that it is almost impossible to part with any more of the natural wealth of Canada in the way we have been doing.
We had an illustration the other day in connection with forests. Hon. members on both sides of the house rose and wanted to preserve our forest resources and timber wealth, and all the other things that flow therefrom, for the people of Canada. We have the same situation as to pipe lines and the Pipe Lines
[Mr. Balcer.J
Act. Will it develop Canada? That should be the first consideration. Is it right, just and proper that we should develop our natural resources for the benefit of other countries? As I said the other day, we had a similar situation with regard to power in the Niagara river. In 1905 the power resources of the Niagara river were under private ownership. Yesterday a return was made in the house- at the moment I have not a copy of it-which referred to the millions of kilowatt hours that were given away by private ownership to the people of the United States. I admit that we owe a great deal to the United States for their kindness and help in both world wars, but nevertheless they are our competitors in an economic way, in a financial way, in a military way. We are even following their social security program to a great extent. We have given first consideration to what is for the benefit of that great nation to the south of us which is more or less our friendly competitor for the wealth of Canada.
You have recently had to consider the question of power in the Niagara river. At the time Sir James Whitney became premier of Ontario, private ownership was giving away pretty nearly all the power in the Niagara river, but when Sir James Whitney came into office in 1905 he cancelled the remaining issues of power which were granted under the Ross-Hardy Liberal government. What did he then do? He instituted what is commonly known as the hydroelectric development, which was a blessing to the people of Canada. Yesterday a return was made in the house-again, I am sorry that I have not a copy at the moment, but I hope to get one shortly-showing the large number of kilowatt hours of power which have been exported from Canada. In Ontario it is a very large amount, and in Quebec it is about the same. I think Ontario has exported more than Quebec to develop industry across the border. The return also referred to the other provinces, and showed that a lesser amount of direct current is generated.
Are we going to continue this policy? I cannot refer to the various clauses of the present bill because it is a composite one. This measure and the bill to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company are the same in principle although the directors are different. This bill was considered in another place the other day, and you will notice that there was a four-line discussion there. That was all that was said on second and third readings. Is that fair? Is that the way to confer a franchise? I hope the house will notice what is being created by this particular bill. You are creating a franchise and giving away the physical assets and natural resources

of Canada. To whom? To private ownership.
My contention is that these great natural resources should belong to the people of Canada so that they may be used for the development of Canada and not for the development of our competitor. While the United States is a friendly nation, and we owe a lot to them, nevertheless they are our friendly competitors. If I had the time I could show the direct saving that has been made in the power of the Niagara river. I should like to quote three or four paragraphs from a speech I made on June 15, 1925, on the export of power. Today the export of power is nearly ten times as great as it was then. The excerpt reads:
1.	Every dollar of the $160 million hydro investment is earning interest and sinking fund.
2.	Hydro investment saved Ontario from a coal famine that would have bankrupted the province in wartime.
That was in 1917.
3.	Hydro investment saved 2,200,000 shareholders over $75 million in reduced coal, light and power bills.
4.	Hydro investment saved Ontario over $100 million on coal prices, which would have gone to $30 per ton in wartime but for the hydro investment that gave Ontario the equivalent of 3,000,000 tons of United States coal per annum.
That is a short story of the development of power on the Niagara river and that value has increased by about ten times today. Now, are we going to give away this franchise? If this bill is sent to a committee I doubt if it will be given any study at all. We had an example of that in connection with another bill two years ago, concerning the Bell Telephone Company; and we saw what happened in that case. That bill was initiated in the other place, which is well named. They seem to consider these bills in a different way over there.
We represent the people of this country, and we have no right to confer a franchise like this. Look at the bill; what does it contain? I cannot refer to the various sections on second reading, but there seems to be a different principle in almost each section. You will see that one section confers power to construct and operate pipe lines for the transmission of gas, oil or any liquid product or by-product. The company is also given power to hold lands. Under various sections of the bill the company is given very wide powers. Then they take out various sections of the Companies Act; in other words, this franchise is conferred upon this private company without the protection afforded by some sections of the Companies Act. Other sections of that act are specifically mentioned; sections 12(7) 39, 40, 59, 62, 63, 64, 65 and 91 of part I of the Companies Act, 1934, are to apply to the company provided that wherever in subsection 7 of section 12 and
Prairie Transmission Lines in section 59 the words "letters patent" or "supplementary letters patent" appear, the words "special act" shall be substituted therefor. So this special act, considered by the Senate, exempts this company from the provisions of certain sections of that general act.
This company is asking a franchise to do what? Well, about the only things that are not covered by the bill are the heavens above, the earth below and the waters beneath the earth. How we can consider a thing like this? Then I call attention to another feature. We are asked to give this company certain privileges and rights which in my opinion should never be given to any company. No one knows just what is involved.. This all follows the adoption of the Pipe Lines Act, which as I said the other evening I think should be called the pipe dream act; I believe that would be a far better title for it. Under that act they can give away anything they like, and now we are asked to confer a franchise upon this company for all time. One of the provisions with respect to the development of power in Ontario was that the people had to vote on all these matters. That protects them when a franchise is sought in the province of Ontario. We have a clause in the municipal act providing that no municipality may give away a franchise without the consent of the ratepayers, and that is good legislation. Many of the younger men in the house came up from the municipalities, the villages, towns and cities. I saw the other day that our honoured and respected Clerk was given a reception and thanked for what he had done for his town in Quebec, and rightly so. I was pleased to see the tribute he was paid in the town from which he comes. Protection such as I have mentioned is a wise step; without the consent of the ratepayers no franchise for the use of the public streets may be granted.
What are these people going to do under this special act? Are they going to rip up the streets? They can do anything they wish. They can transmit anything they like across the border, to help build up the economy of the United States. Our two countries are supposed to be friendly competitors in trade. Eaton's and Simpson's are friendly rivals for trade, but they are also good businessmen. So are these people in the United States who are our competitors. If this is the way business is done in the other place, I think some changes should be made. In connection with the bill to which I was referring the other evening, I had the report of proceedings in the Senate. The bill was introduced, sent to committee, reported back and put through, and the whole procedure only took up three or four lines in Hansard. If that is the way they confer franchises I am surprised at the

Prairie Transmission Lines high court of parliament, and I can only say that is not the way to part with the wealth of this country.
Years ago Houston's Annual used to be a textbook in all the stock exchanges across the country. Now they have a different book with a blue cover, listing all companies and showing their affiliations with each other. What does that book show? It shows the way these companies are interlocked. I looked up some of these points not long ago, and found that all our natural wealth along the Ottawa river is owned and financed in New York. The timber, the gold, the silver, the platinum, the zinc, the asbestos and all the other things are shipped out in raw form, and there manufactured into finished articles, providing employment for thousands of men and producing wealth amounting to millions of dollars. Is that the way for us to build up this country? How are we going to develop our natural resources under such a policy? Is that the way to create employment? Do not forget that we may run into a depression. Nobody can tell. It may come like a thief in the night. Is that the way to create employment? I say no. What we have to do is to veto these bills. There is no use talking about friendly competitors in these days.
The question is, are you going to give over the natural resources and the natural wealth of this country to private people to exploit for gain, or are you going to reserve the natural resources of our country-I have only mentioned a few of them-for the development of our country. I believe in a policy of Canada for Canadians, trade and industry and everything else. Our own work for our own workmen; our own markets for our own products; that is the policy in which I believe. I believe that policy has built up this country. For those reasons, I am going to vote against second reading of the bill. No one else is prepared to move a six months' hoist oh the principle of the bill. If I can get a seconder, I shall be glad to move that this bill be read a second time on a date six months from today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill merits the *careful consideration of the members of the house. This evening I propose to say a few words about it. In the first place, a word about some terms of the bill which is, as all members know, a bill to incorporate a company known as the Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. The men who are applying for the incorporation are five in number, and are all solicitors, either of Toronto or of Ottawa.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. mem-oer should discuss the principle of the bill

at this time. The hon. member is now referring to a section of the bill, and on second reading the principle should be discussed.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
I mentioned the applicants for incorporation because I propose to bring that into my submission at a later stage. It is quite obvious that the applicants are merely acting for some other interests.
The bill gives this proposed company the power to construct and operate a pipe line, for both natural gas and oil. By virtue of a statute passed at the session of the house last spring, which was known as the Pipe Lines Act, if this company receives incorporation, it will have the very wide powers outlined in that foundation bill. For example, it will have wide power to enter on property to make surveys and construct a pipe line, and it will have extremely wide powers of expropriation. One other feature about the terms of the bill itself is that the company is given these powers within the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia or outside Canada.
Before continuing, I think something should be said about what happened in this house last spring. Those members who survived the holocaust of June 27 will remember that the Pipe Lines Act was brought into the house a day or two before prorogation. At the same time several of these private bills were brought in, under which approximately five different companies were eventually incorporated. At that stage in the session it was impossible to give careful consideration either to the foundation bill or to those private bills.
Members will recall that the private bills were referred to the standing committee on railways, canals, and telegraph lines. During one of the evenings of the last week of the session there was a meeting of the committee which lasted about half an hour. The men representing the various companies were present and gave brief explanations. I think the committee took an average of about five or ten minutes on each of those private bills. I do not believe anyone can dispute the fact that this house did not have an opportunity in April to give careful consideration either to the Pipe Lines Act or to any of those private bills. Everything was put through in great haste. We were told that the Imperial Oil had to commence laying the pipe line from Edmonton to Regina at once, and that if the bills were not put through western Canada would suffer.
The time has now come, Mr. Speaker, when it is the duty of this house to give more careful consideration to pipe line bills. I think it is our duty to insist that this bill, or any legislation that goes through the house from now on dealing with pipe lines, must be in

the best form possible. It need not necessarily be in exactly the same form as the legislation which went through in such a hurry last April. I suggest to the house that there are several things that should be taken care of in legislation of this type.
In the first place, the general route that is to be followed by the pipe line should be set out in each of these bills. If we pass this bill in its present form, we are giving a blank cheque to the company. In the case of some of the bills, we are simply saying, "You can build a pipe line anywhere in Canada," and in the case of this particular bill we are saying, "You can instal a pipe line anywhere in Alberta or British Columbia". It certainly is the responsibility of parliament to go into the question in more detail than that, and to decide the approximate route the pipe line should take.
I should like to point out what happened in connection with this particular bill when it was before the other place. I do wish, Mr. Speaker, we were allowed to say the Senate; it would be more understandable. When this bill was before the other place, the sponsor explained the route of this particular pipe line. The members will find that on page 117 of the Senate Hansard.
The sponsors of the bill are Canadians; they have completed their engineering studies for the construction of the pipe line, and propose to transport gas across a corner of British Columbia, up to Trail, and through to the coast at a point near Seattle,-
Which is, of course, in the United States.
-and thence up to Vancouver.
Now, that was the statement made in the Senate. But when the bill was introduced in this house the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) told a different story. As reported at page 1344 of Hansard, this is what he said:
I wish to make it clear that the passing of this bill does not in any way establish routes for the transmission lines for this company.
Then on the next page he said:
I should like to inform the house that the bill has nothing to do with routes. There is nothing in it that establishes a route.
If we turn back to the days when railway charters were being granted by parliament, we find that in the incorporating statute the routes were set out. I have here the statutes for 1902, containing an act known as chapter 62, an act to incorporate the Essex Terminal Railway Company. It constitutes certain men a corporation but it has a paragraph which sets out the line of railway authorized; that is section 8, which reads as follows:
The company may lay out, construct and operate a railway, of the gauge of four feet eight and one-half inches, from a point in or near the town of
Prairie Transmission Lines Walkerville, through the townships of Sandwich East and Sandwich West, and the city of Windsor, to some point in or near the town of Sandwich, and through the town of Sandwich, the townships of Sandwich West and Anderdon to a point in or near the town of Amherstburg.
Then I have here another act. This time the petitioner was the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is chapter 79 of the statutes of 1919. It gives the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the authority to build seven different lines of railway but in each case says approximately where that line is to go. Finally, I have here the statutes of 1924. In chapter 82 we find an act to incorporate Joliette and Northern Railway Company. It is the same type of act. It constitutes certain men a corporation. Then there is this section which sets out where the line of railway must go. Section 9 reads as follows:
The company may lay out, construct and operate a railway of the gauge of four feet eight and one-half inches from a point in or near the town of Joliette, in the county of Joliette, in the province of Quebec, in a north by northwesterly direction to a point in or near the village of St. Michel des Saints in the county of Berthier, and thence by the most feasible route to a point on the National Transcontinental Railway at or near Parent, a distance of about one hundred and sixty miles.
That has been the practice followed with railways, and I suggest that we should adopt the same practice with regard to these pipe lines. This house cannot decide on the merits of these applications for statutes incorporating a private company unless the members of the house know where the pipe line is to go. It is not good enough to have somebody read in the paper that it is going to be in such and such an area.
The same point was raised in the other place in a debate on October 4, that debate being on the other pipe line bill, incorporating the Alberta Natural Gas Company. There Hon. Mr. Hugessen raised this point. At page 81 of the debates of the Senate he is reported to have said:
I was just wondering whether the bills we passed last year specifically stated the particular area in which the companies intended to build.
And he went on to say:
I think in the future that parliament should take care to see that this is done.
I submit this evening therefore that we should take care to see that in each one of these private bills there is written in the area in which the pipe line is to be laid.
There is another provision which I suggest should be written into this legislation, and that is a provision to the effect that Canadian requirements must be met first by the companies before they export their product to the United States. There is a provision of that type in a statute known as the Electricity

Prairie Transmission Lines and Fluid Exportation Act, which is chapter 54 of the Revised Statutes of Canada of 1927. There we find it written into the act:
Any such licence-
That is any licence for the export of fluid.

may provide that the quantity of power or fluid-
Which fluid would include gas and oil.
-to be exported shall be limited to the surplus, after the licensee has supplied for distribution to customers for use in Canada power or fluid to the extent defined by such licence, at prices and in accordance with conditions, rules and regulations prescribed by the governor in council.
My submission is that some provision of that type should be written into each one of these private bills.
In the case of the bill we are now discussing there is of course no attempt whatever to meet the requirements of Canada before exporting to the United States. The statement made in the Senate shows that the pipe line is to go from southern Alberta through the Crowsnest pass into British Columbia, and then down into the United States at the first convenient place. Once it goes into the United States it will go to Spokane and eventually to Seattle and Portland.
In the Senate there was a suggestion that there would be a branch of this pipe line up into Trail in the valley of the Columbia river in Canada. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much whether that would be done. Certainly the main object is to get into Washington and Oregon. The suggestion is made that eventually this pipe line will reach Vancouver. It may or it may not. There may or may not be any gas left over by the time it gets to Vancouver, and the United States authorities may or may not permit that pipe . line to come back into Canada once it has gone into the United States. I doubt very much whether they would give that permission.
In any event, the pipe line certainly will be of little value to any other part of British Columbia. Actually, in going through the Crowsnest pass it will put gas in competition with the coal industry in that pass. As hon. members from British Columbia know, the Crowsnest district depends largely on coal for employment. If this bill is passed, and if this company goes ahead as is suggested, the result will be the development of Washington and Oregon. I would point out that it is not only gas that is involved. They are also taking the power to pipe oil there. If they pipe oil, then we shall have refineries established down in Spokane or Seattle, giving employment to Americans, and Canada can just wait or possibly the west coast can continue indefinitely

to import her oil from the United States. It would mean giving employment to Americans instead of to Canadians.
The situation is even worse than that because British Columbia is in direct competition with Washington and Oregon. Our lumbermen have to compete with lumbermen of Washington and Oregon. Our fishermen compete with the fishermen of Washington and Oregon. Our fruit growers are in competition with fruit growers down the same valleys in Washington. You may well have the position that the Americans in competition with us are getting Canadian gas and Canadian oil while the people in British Columbia cannot get these commodities.
The bill which was passed last session did not have that objection, because that company's line was to come from northern Alberta down through the province of British Columbia, serving practically every community in that province, and once it served Vancouver and New Westminster nobody could have any objection to the surplus being exported to the United States. There was a plan which I suggest was in the best interest of Canada. For that reason the bill passed last session without any opposition whatever.
I repeat, there should be written into these acts some provision that Canadian requirements are to be met first. The premier of Alberta has taken that stand. During previous debates letters from him have been read in the house. One of them will be found at page 1345 of Hansard. In that letter he pointed out the requirements of the government of Alberta before they would issue a licence. The third requirement was:
It will be a condition of any export permit that Canadian requirements must be given first priority.
I am asking that that condition be put in this bill, and that in every pipe-line bill there should be a condition that Canadian requirements must be given first priority. The suggestion will be made that that can be left to the board of transport commissioners. Mr. Speaker, it is not the job of the board of transport commissioners to lay down a policy of that kind. If that is the policy of the government it should be laid down in a statute by parliament and not just left to the board of transport commissioners.
May I mention something else in connection with these pipe-line bills. I believe that hon. members should be very careful to see that these bills are not merely in furtherance of a promotion scheme. There is big money involved in this business. In a few months or a year's time we may find that we have granted these charters to some solicitors and that they were acting for some promoters,

and that these promotors have sold the charters for hundreds of thousands of dollars. That is a situation against which this house must guard. Let the people who are really behind these applications for private bills come into this house and ask for incorporation themselves so that we may know to whom we are giving these rights. If there are big oil companies involved let us know about them. When a company was incorporated last spring to build a pipe line from Edmonton to Regina we were told that the Imperial Oil Company was behind that company; that it was in effect a subsidiary of the Imperial Oil Company. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) may correct me if I am wrong in this, but there was another private bill incorporating a company known as the British American Pipe Line Company. We were told that that company was a subsidiary of several of the major oil companies. Hon. members had that information. But in the case of the bill now before us we have no idea whatever who is behind it.

I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the wise way for this house to handle these bills is to insist on being told such facts before approving the bill. These names should appear right in the bill itself. If that were done there could be no misunderstanding and there could be no fast footwork. We would know with whom we were dealing.
There is another thing we should remember about this bill. While the power is taken to carry oil, it is primarily a natural gas pipe line, and under the Pipe Lines Act, which was passed last session, the companies that carry natural gas are not common carriers. Companies that carry oil are common carriers, they have to carry oil produced by anybody who offers it for carriage, or however you describe the movement of oil. But that is not so with these natural gas pipes lines. They are not common carriers.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED

It may be that they cannot be common carriers, although we did not have time last session to go into that question
Prairie Transmission Lines carefully. I point out to hon. members that if this company is incorporated and puts in a natural gas pipe line it will be under no obligation whatever to carry natural gas for any other company.
I know the suggestion will be made-in fact it has already been made-that we should give incorporation to anybody who wishes to come here and ask for a private bill, and let them compete. That would be a very unwise way to handle the situation. It would in effect mean that parliament acts purely as a rubber stamp, granting incorporation to anybody and then letting them fight it out. I do not believe that we can evade our responsibility in that way. I suggest that it is the duty of hon. members to go carefully into the facts in each of these applications for incorporation, and then to decide on the merits of the particular application.
Therefore I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the house should vote down this bill. It is a private bill. Government policy is not involved. All we are dealing with is the application of five solicitors to be made a company and to be given these tremendously wide powers. There can be no question of a vote against the bill being a vote of want of confidence in the government. I hope hon. members will vote against the bill. That would mean that in the months intervening between the end of this session and the beginning of the next one further consideration could be given to the points I have raised and those raised by other hon. members in these pipe line debates. There will be far more time next session also to consider these bills in committee. For these reasons therefore I do urge that this bill be voted down.

subtopic: PRAIRIE TRANSMISSION LINES LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to attempt to shorten the debate by calling the attention of hon. members to the situation that faces parliament when dealing with these applications. This is not an application to build a pipe line; it is simply an application to incorporate a company that would like to build a pipe line. If the incorporation is granted the next step must be for the company to sign up sufficient production of natural gas or to acquire natural gas in some way, in quantity sufficient to justify the pipe line.
The third step is that the company must obtain from the province of Alberta a licence to export gas from that province. That step is really the key to the whole situation, since the company that receives the licence to export gas from Alberta will be the company that builds the pipe line for gas. And may I say in passing that I am very glad indeed,

Prairie Transmission Lines as a member of this government, that the province of Alberta has relieved this government of the responsibility of making a choice of pipe line companies to do this particular job.
The next step is this: the company, having sufficient gas to warrant a pipe line and having a licence from Alberta to export that gas, must come before the board of transport commissioners and satisfy the requirements of the Pipe Lines Act. It must prove to the board convenience and necessity. It must show that the project is properly financed. It must show that supplies of gas within the control of the company are sufficient to warrant a pipe line, and it must obtain the approval of the board of transport commissioners regarding a route.
But that is not all. The board of transport commissioners will, I assume, as they have in the past, require that the company produce a licence under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act which is administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The purpose of that act is to see that resources of Canada, such as power or fluids or gas, which depend upon continuous transport, are used primarily for the benefit of Canada. That act was passed by this parliament at a time when it was found that, in the past, electricity produced in Canada and needed in Canada had been alienated by long-term contracts made with users in the United States.
In my opinion the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act is one of the most important acts on our statute books. I believe the administration of the act has prevented alienation of Canada's natural resources, such as had been taking place before the act was placed on the statute books.
A good deal has been said about the route of these two pipe lines. All I know about the route is that one of the groups asking for incorporation visited me and asked what the attitude of the government would be regarding administration of the exportation act to which I have referred. I stated that the attitude of the government would be that the export of gas would be treated in exactly the same way that we treat the export of electricity, namely that the needs of Canada would be served first and would be protected in perpetuity for all export purposes.

Neither could it happen in a House of Commons more evenly divided between government and opposition members than is the present one. I suggest that points to the error in the decision made by the government, and also to the tragedy of this parliament. The tragedy of this parliament is that its overwhelming government majority is becoming more and more detached from the people of Canada whom it is supposed to represent.

The way hon. members are acting in the house shows that they have completely forgotten the relationship with the people of their constituencies which they promised they would maintain. Those things must surely impress upon Liberal members of the house that what the people back home want is that their representatives shall live up to their promises, and that parHament shall somehow represent the wishes and desires of the Canadian people.
It seems to me there ought not to be this difference between a House of Commons that is evenly divided and a house that has an overwhelming majority on one side. It is still the elected house in the parliament of Canada; and the job of hon. members, whether they are on the minority or the majority side, is to think of the wishes and desires of the people of their constituencies. What happens? Some hon. members went home for the week end, and they got the feeling of their constituents. They told newspaper writers either in their home towns or after they came back to Ottawa that this was a hot issue. The newspaper writers were able to put stories in the papers to the effect that there would be a real commotion within Liberal ranks, that Liberals would be calling upon the government to rescind the order, or certainly to make very drastic changes in it.
We understood today that once the debate was under way certain Liberals would take part in it, but such has not been the case. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gets
up and makes a very fine speech; Liberal members applaud, and somehow or other they are mesmerized into thinking the situation is not so bad after all. I ask any Liberal member to get a reprint of the speech made by the Minister of Finance this afternoon, send it to the people of his constituency who are complaining, and ask them to use it to pay the increased rent. Ask them to read that speech and see if it makes them feel as satisfied as some hon. members felt this afternoon, simply because the minister lulled them back into their accustomed complacency. I challenge hon. members again to get away from being mesmerized by the feeling they are in power with an overwhelming majority. The Manitoba government is loath to take over rental control, Premier D. L. Campbell said in a statement read by Educational Minister C. Rhodes Smith last night during a radio address.

I think Premier Campbell is right when he says that rental controls are more easily and efficiently administered by one government rather than by ten provincial governments, but I hope the people of Manitoba realize they are now being handed the same kind of half assurances that they were given by the Liberals prior to the 27th of June. Once the 10th of November is past, any thought that the Manitoba government would take over rent control in that province is just

Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go much further, but there is one thing the minister has tried to say both ways to which 1 want to call attention. That is not what Canadians voted for on June 27. That is not what the Liberal members of this house promised to do for the people of Canada by Christmas t^iis year.
