speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate with considerable interest, and I should like to preface my remarks by saying that this question is not a political issue. It is not a Liberal nor a Tory nor a C.C.F. issue. It boils down to cold, hard economic facts and a little bit of honesty. If we intend to relieve the people of this country who are going to be affected by this action-and around four million are affected-if we honestly want to do something for them and face the economic facts, then it is not good enough to follow party tactics. Nor is it good enough for the government, with their large majority, to sit back complacently and say, "Well, we are here for four more years. The memory of the people is short. Before the next election we will give them a few little palliatives and they will forget all about this." That seems to be the feeling. You know, Mr. Speaker, I do not like the truculent attitude of the members of the government in chucking their weight around. It pays to be humble in victory; when you stick up your head too far somebody is going to knock it off for you. If you keep it down and show a little honesty in your thinking on questions which come before you, in which there is merit, I think the people of Canada will have a great deal more respect for this institution.
There is a great deal of merit in this question. The whole matter is one of control, and we do not need to guess about the problem any longer. When this country faced a crisis in the early days of the war there was no quibbling about it. We then had a national objective, the winning of the war. It was a matter of survival, and neither the members of this house nor the cabinet sat back and said, "We are just going to let this thing go along in a haphazard way." It required a certain amount of planning. The first thing the government decided must be done was the holding of prices somewhere within reason; and they made a very good job of it. From the start of the war until about the end of 1941 prices were uncontrolled, and in that period they jumped about 15-8 points. So the government instituted controls. They fought the war; they allocated materials; they controlled prices; and up to the end of 1945, when the war was over, the price index had gone up only about 4-3 points.
In defending controls in this house Mr. Ilsley made the statement that by means of controls he had saved the people of this country some $12,500 million, or approximately $1,000 for every man, woman and

Rent Control
child in Canada. That was good business, was it not? No one was hurt; no one transacting business during that period suffered; their profits were within reason, and every person in this country benefited to the extent of a thousand dollars. Then came the end of the war and we wanted to get back to the things that caused the war; the unplanned, unrestricted economy, where greed and avarice are the motivating factors in society; and that is where we went.
The minister speaks of orderly decontrol. Beginning in 1946 controls were removed. Our opinion was that they were never more badly needed than during the transition from war to peace. We had an effective machinery administered by experienced men; and the worth of that machinery had been proved during the war. But in 1946 the minister said he was going to go ahead with it in an orderly fashion, so controls came off; and from early in 1946 until about the end of 1947 the price index jumped by some 25 -9 points. In other words prices rose by only 4-3 points in the whole process of fighting the war; then in a little more than a year after the end of the war, when controls began to be removed, the index soared by 25 -9 points. I believe that increase indicates to hon. members that price controls should have been maintained during that period. It must be remembered that industry in this country went through a great deal of upheaval, trouble, strikes and misery, because when prices began to skyrocket wages began to chase them. If controls had been maintained during the period I have just mentioned, and prices kept within reason, we would have avoided that disruption of industry. It would have been good business, and it should have been done.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Including wage control?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Wages were controlled. Certainly you must have a measure of wage control if you are going to have price control. We have never denied that. In fact we have advocated it, and it was accepted during the war. Today the cost of living index stands at around 160. I believe it was 160-1, but it dropped a little. There has been a terrific increase in the cost of living. The people that I have in mind in this particular instance are the people in the low-income brackets. A large percentage of our people do not pay income taxes, and those are the people who live in rented houses. Those are the people who are going to suffer most under this rent increase.
An estimate made by the Toronto welfare council reveals that the small-income groups in this country spend at least fifty-five per cent of their total income on food. In the matter of rents, the landlords received a
[Mr Gillis.]
rent increase of 10 per cent about a year ago. I believe that this last gesture on the part of the minister was ill-considered. I am not going to kick the minister around for it because I know him quite well. I know his background, and he came up the hard way. The minister may be on top of the heap today, but I believe he has some bad advisers in the background. I think he should look them over carefully. This move was badly timed, very badly timed.
I do not think the government should have made a move at this time. They have not exactly removed the control from rents but, in effect, they have told the landlords of this country they are justified in increasing rents by 20 or 25 per cent. I believe that was a wrong approach to the problem. If the minister was going to do anything about it, it would have been better for him to vacate the field completely and leave out of the picture that matter of instructing the landlords as to the percentage by which they could increase rents. The minister says they do not have to increase rents by that amount. The fact of the matter is that the landlords will charge it. Examples of that can be found in this house.
I know a person employed in the civil service who had an apartment for which he was paying $30 per month. When certain types of accommodation were decontrolled, he had to get out immediately. He went into an apartment which before the war rented for around $45 per month. The landlord split it up and made two apartments out of it. This man who was paying $30 per month rent, all he could afford, was forced to pay $85 per month for one end of that apartment. The other end was rented for $75 per month. That landlord was receiving $160 per month for accommodation which, in 1939, rented for $45 per month. That was under decontrol. You will find a large percentage of the landlords will take that attitude and say, "Well, Mr. Abbott said twenty-five per cent for this type of accommodation. Rents will be increased by twenty-five per cent. It would have been much better if the federal government had vacated the field and said nothing about the rent increase.
I believe that housing is this country's No. 1 problem in many respects. It is the No. 1 problem in the field of employment. The lumber industry is rather stagnant; the steel mills are not producing as they should; the fuel industry is down and the building trades are not all employed. I believe Canada should set up a low-rental housing program as a national objective. This would provide us with an incentive such as we had during the war. This country has no objective now. In this House of Commons we

are roaming around like a ship without a rudder. Someone on the government benches should set a low-rental subsidized housing program as an objective to cure the housing problem of the low-income groups. Until such time as that is done, nothing will help our people. It would stimulate the lumber industry and the steel industry and put the building trades to work. It would create employment and new wealth for this country. I think that is an objective for which we could all work. It is not a Liberal or a C.C.F. objective; it is a common-sense approach to our No. 1 problem.
Then the question arises, where are you going to get the money? Before the war that question was heard quite often. There was no money for relief or anything else. Immediately upon the outbreak of war, instead of appropriating millions we were appropriating billions-we were even making gifts of billions. There is money. I am going to name one particular spot from which we could get some money. These figures were taken from the public accounts and concern subsidies that were paid up to 1945. The total subsidies amounted to $210,591,000. The administration of the wartime prices and trade board cost $14 million in 1945. That sounds like a lot of money.
Immediately after the war excess profits taxes were abolished. The yearly revenue from those taxes amounted to $465,805,356 per year. That is also a lot of money. If the government is in earnest about solving the low-rental housing problem of this country on a subsidized basis, I believe it would cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $120 million per year. Is it unreasonable to say that the excess profits tax should be reimposed in an amount sufficient to offset a subsidized housing program for this country?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Is he aware that the British Labour government removed the excess profits tax on industry one year before this government did, for reasons which the Chancellor of the Exchequer gave at that time?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The tax rate in the United Kingdom is much higher and they also have a capital gains tax which we have not got.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that, when the Canadian government removed the excess profits tax, it followed the same procedure as the United Kingdom and increased the standard rate of corporation taxation from 18 per cent to 30 per cent?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I was not aware of that.
Rent Control

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I suggest you do a little research about your Labour government in Great Britain.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I have done a little research, and it appears to be hurting. Your questions do not bother me at all.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The answers bother you.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have no objection to the hon. member asking those questions because he just gets his feet wet all the time. There is no comparison between Britain and Canada. I have heard the Prime Minister and other members in this house say that we are much better off than any other country in the world. I think that is childish and nonsensical. Britain was devastated by war. She came out with perhaps a million of her people in airraid shelters. The United Kingdom imports practically everything the people eat or wear as well as all building materials. The same thing applies to the rest of Europe. You cannot compare this country, which covers half a continent, has unlimited resources, thirteen million people and never a scar of war, to a country like Britain. We built up our standards while they were tearing theirs down. There is no comparison at all. We are better off, certainly, but I would not want to go through what the people of Britain went through with the same kind of administration we have today, and expect it to drag us out of fthe ruins of war. I think the comparison is one which hon. members would not want to put on the record.
I was just pointing out, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the minister who just entered the chamber, that in this matter of removing controls-I have said a lot about it and I am not going to repeat it-I thought that the success of the whole control structure during the war, the benefits that the Canadian people derived from it and the excellent job that was done by the administration in that field, was attributable to the fact that this country at that time had a national objective, which was the winning of the war. It was not a Liberal war, a Tory war, or a C.C.F. war. We all got into it and helped to win it. You laid down certain mechanism that worked during the war.
I make this suggestion to the minister. He is a military man and knows that you have got to have objectives if you are going to go into a battle; you must choose a battleground, plan your attack and so forth. I think we now need another national objective, and that we shall have to reconstitute some of the machinery with which we were so successful in fighting the war. I made this suggestion. I am repeating this for the minister's benefit. I know he is receptive

Rent Control
and sympathetic, and that if ideas are right he will perhaps put them into operation. I suggest that our housing problem in this country is our No. 1 problem and that we should all forget our party politics and should set as our objective the elimination of slums and the establishment of a good, low-rental, subsidized housing program as the only means of relieving the low-income groups and giving them housing. I think we should say that should be done. It would stimulate production. Your lumber industry would work on it. Your steel mills would work on it. Your building trades would go to work. It would create employment and solve our No. 1 problem.
Someone may ask where we are going to get the money for all this. I pointed out the amount of subsidies-according to the public accounts report of 1945, some $210 million was paid out; the administration of the wartime prices and trade board cost about $14 million, in round figures; but at the same time your excess profits tax that you had used during the war in order to finance the war was yielding the government some $465 million, in round figures again. According to figures I have seen, a subsidy of about $120 million a year would provide an adequate low-rental housing program in this country. I ask the members of the house if it is unreasonable to reimpose an excess profits tax to gather sufficient revenue to provide that subsidy. I do not think you would have hurt anyone because I think that normal profits, without extra profits, are sufficient. I think the balance sheets of companies and corporations throughout Canada during the war show that they were making a fair and reasonable profit as determined by the finance department. That huge amount of money that was handed back to them in excess profits is not being used. They do not need it. I suggest to the minister that he appeal to all members in this house to forget their party differences; let us tap that resource in order to get a sufficient amount of money to provide a low-rental subsidized housing program, make it a national objective at this time, and get behind it and push it.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) issue a challenge to this side of the house, Mr. Speaker. He inquired why more so-called Liberal backbenchers were not getting up to speak on this subject. As a rule, I do not like to allow a challenge to go unheeded. I am therefore taking this one up. To the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who mentioned the fact that he thought we were getting out of touch with the people, I should like to say

that he should remember that not so long ago we were very much in touch with the people, and I think we still are. I believe that the right-thinking people of Canada- the people who do not, for instance, take advantage of a debate like this to practise demagoguery and to bring forward a program of "soak the rich"-are inclined to agree with this government which they elected not so long ago and in which I am sure they still have confidence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Does the hon. member think that the people support these rental increases?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I think that the majority of the people do. They are not rental increases, as a matter of fact, and I think that the majority of the people support the policy of the government which I will attempt to explain in a few minutes if my hon. friend will bear with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We believe in a fair deal for all.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: One of the members on the other side of the house said that it was not a political issue. By no stretch of the imagination can this government be accused of playing politics with this issue.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: They are certainly not taking the easy way and they are certainly not trying to take what they might have reason to believe would be the most popular course with the people-

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: After the election.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: -or with the tenants, who after all are the majority in certain of our large cities. But I wish to say that, as the government is not playing politics, it is at the same time being consistent. The government is doing no more than carrying out the policy that was laid before the people in the last election, and that policy was supported. I see that my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre looks surprised.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I am surprised.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I will attempt to establish that fact. In the last election the government said that it was in favour of doing away with all wartime controls. It has been the policy of this government for some time to do away with all wartime controls. One of the wartime controls, and the only one remaining, was rent control. The government and the speakers who spoke for the government-and I was one-said that in due course the rental controls would be removed. Now the rental controls are being removed. Things are perhaps going a little

bit faster than was expected. I will admit that; nevertheless the government is taking the courageous action it said it would take, and it is being even more courageous than it possibly had to be under all circumstances. As I said before, it cannot be accused of playing politics nor of taking the easy way. When one is governing, one must remember -and if my hon. friends on the other side of the house ever have to govern, which I hope will not happen in my time, they will realize it-that it is more difficult to do the right thing than to do the popular thing.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is hard to be a statesman.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The hon. member will never succeed.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The government is carrying out this program of removing controls, and is also taking another method of doing away with the disadvantage that lessees suffered from because of high rents, with a housing program. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) talked about having a subsidized housing program. We have a housing program which has been explained to us by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) and it is going forward. Under it we have built more houses and have done more to relieve the shortage of dwellings than any other country has done since the war. That fact should not be forgotten.
Something was said about newspaper writers. I read the reports in the Standard also. I read all the declarations made by the members from Montreal, and I was particularly struck by the unanimity of those declarations. They all said one thing and one thing only, namely, that they were in favour of retaining rent controls for the present. Who is not? We are. We are retaining rent controls for the present. We have lifted the ceiling but we are retaining rent controls, and that is all the hon. members said. It cannot be said that one of these hon. members made any statement that was not in conformity with the policy of the government as it has been established by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). We must not lose our sense of proportion. After all, this is a decision that shocks some people, but it is not the end of the world. It is not the end of this parliament; it is not even the end of the Liberal party. Talking about not losing a sense of proportion, I should like to re-establish some figures that the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) did not seem to quite understand this afternoon. I refer to the maximum increases which are authorized. As was explained by
Rent Control
the Minister of Finance, to whom I listened this afternoon, the total is 40 per cent as the limit, not 45 per cent. First, 10 per cent, then 5 per cent and then 25 per cent, which makes 40 per cent.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You work it out.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Forty per cent only. The minister said this afternoon that when you calculated the 10 per cent you calculated it on 100 per cent. When you added 5 per cent you did not add it on to 110 per cent, you added it on to 100 per cent. When you added 25 per cent you did not add it on to 115 per cent, you added it on to 100 per cent, and that makes 40 per cent. Let us consider this in a dispassionate manner. Let us take the figures as they are and let us not lose our sense of proportion. We are not losing our sense of proportion. The important thing to my mind is the proportion of rent to wages.
I challenge any hon. members on the other side to prove that this is not true, even with the increase that is now going into effect, if it goes into effect and rents are increased to the maximum authorized. Even if rents are increased up to the limit authorized the proportion of rent to wages will not be any higher than it was in 1939. The proportion of rent paid by the working man on the average in proportion to his total wages is not any higher now than it was then. So, where is the great hardship? There is no great hardship there; it is just a matter of readjustment.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You mean you want to get back to the 1939 conditions?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I did not say I want to get back to the 1939 conditions. I am asking hon. members not to lose their sense of proportion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Like you have.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: He has not any.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There is another angle to be considered in this. I take it, it will not be popular with hon. members on the other side, but one must consider that the government and the rent controls have to be fair to the land owners. After all, they are citizens of this country and like any others they are entitled to be fairly treated. Evidently hon. members on the other side do not want them to be fairly treated; but I believe it is the duty of this government to treat all classes of citizens in this country equally fairly. If the land owners are fairly treated they are getting only their due. If the ceiling were not raised we would be in this situation. We would be taxing illegally one section of the population of this country; we would be discriminating against one class whom we would be forcing to bear the burden of the benefits

Rent Control
that the tenants are deriving from the fact that the rents are not allowed to go up. Who would have to pay for that? So far, the property owners. I say that is not fair. I say it is not fair to tax one class of the population in this country so as to benefit another class. That is the policy of the Liberal party. That is the policy they have had the courage to put into force by the regulations that have been made.
Another point that should not be lost sight of is that after all rent control is a provincial responsibility. There can be no doubt whatever about that. For the moment I am speaking as a lawyer. If anyone looks at the B.N.A. Act he can see that property and civil rights are a provincial responsibility.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Why take it to court, then?

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I shall explain that in a minute. Property and civil rights are a provincial responsibility. There is no doubt about that. What can be more within the scope of property and civil rights than rent? Rents have to do with real estate, which is property, and the civil rights of the land owners who rent to the lessees, and the civil rights of the lessees who rent from the landlord. There is no doubt at all that that comes squarely within property and civil rights.
To answer my hon. friend's question, during the war, because of the emergency, the federal government assumed control with the consent of the provinces, if not the explicit consent, at least the tacit consent; and we still have their consent evidently because they will not take the responsibility themselves.
Another thing that we should consider when talking about the responsibility of the provinces is that not only is it a legal responsibility but in all fairness they should take it because conditions are different in different provinces. It is not a matter on which the federal government can legislate for the whole of Canada. It is a matter which should be legislated upon in the different provinces where conditions vary. Conditions in my province of Quebec are not the same as they are in Ontario. Conditions in British Columbia are not the same as they are in the prairies. Everybody knows that. From there it is easy to conclude that it is a matter that should be taken up by the provinces. I understand that the province of Saskatchewan has some stand-by legislation, and that it is ready to assume its responsibility. Evidently it is the only province in Canada that has done so. Since my hon. friend's party is in power there, I take the opportunity of congratulating them on having done that, but the other provinces ought to do it also. There is no doubt that it is a provincial responsibility.

It is an unfortunate situation. Everybody agrees that it is an unfortunate situation, but it is an unfortunate situation that had to come sooner or later. The policy of the government was decontrol.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Orderly decontrol.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The policy of the government is to give up the control of rents. They are giving it up. It is an unfortunate situation, but the government is not wholly responsible for it. As I pointed out before, those who are really responsible for this situation are the provinces who refuse to assume their responsibility.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I say that I think we ought to be thankful in place of criticizing the government, in place of trying to make things difficult for the government, which has taken on its responsibilities like a man. We should be thankful that we have a government which is taking its responsibilities-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Shirking them.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: -that are not rightfully its under the British North America Act. I turn the word "shirking" back to my hon. friend. I will say to him that it is the provinces who are shirking their responsibilities.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: You will be sorry you made that speech.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from the city of Vancouver, which is perhaps one of the most overcrowded cities in the Dominion of Canada, I cannot very well let this debate go by without saying something about the issues involved and how it is going to affect the people in my part of the country.
I believe the psychologists say that you can always know the environment in which people were brought up by their reactions to certain conditions or circumstances. People who live in isolated places will not understand the problems of congested cities where large numbers of people have to live in poverty. The member who just preceded me said that this was a very unfortunate situation. I agree with him, that it is an unfortunate situation, because it will affect people-as every other increase in the cost of living has affected people-who would find it difficult to get along even if there were no increase in the cost of living. It will affect the poor. It will not affect the members of this House of Commons. It will not affect people in Canada who are getting $6,000 a year or more. But, as I can show hon. members, it will affect mothers who are trying to bring up families of several children on incomes of less than $100 a

month. Under circumstances such as that, any increase, no matter how small, means that those women and children will have less to eat.
That is why it is unfortunate. I am not going to belabour the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I will agree at once that some landlords have been getting a bad deal, and that some attempt should have been made to find a way to help them. But when the minister calls the removal of controls to the extent of 20 and 25 per cent orderly decontrol, he is just talking nonsense. I am not so sure it would not have been better to remove controls altogether. I am not saying that it would, but I am saying that -

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Just a moment, now; that is no joke.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No, it is not.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am saying the probability is that every landlord who raises his rent will raise it the full amount allowed by law. That is what is likely to happen. He will say "the government allows a 25 per cent increase, and I am going to take it."
It was refreshing to find one member of the Liberal party, apart from the minister, who had the hardihood, even if inexperienced, to rise in his place in defence of the government. Oh, I could name a good many members in the house whom I did not see rising to their feet with a rush to defend the action of the government. I look over at them, and I could name quite a number of them; but out of consideration for their feelings and the fact that I know them, and know they are good fellows, I shall not mention their constituencies.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And they are very grateful to you.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But that is the picture. We have heard it said that he who runs may read. Well, you can run pretty darned fast during the past few days and read the protests from one end of this country to the other. When we have opponents of controls such as the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Star writing long editorials on the folly of this decontrol, you can rest assured-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Just the Montreal Gazette, I think.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
No, the Montreal Star. I believe it was the Montreal Star reporter who drew my attention to it yesterday afternoon as I was walking along the corridor. I took occasion to have the page bring the paper in the chamber to me, and I read it here. It was the Montreal Star,
Rent Control

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The Montreal Standard raised its price the same day the changes were made in rent controls.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Why not? If the Minister of Finance considered the people of Canada to be in such good circumstances that he could allow the removal of rent controls, why should not the Montreal Standard increase the price of its product, as well?
I would draw the attention of the house and the minister to the situation in Vancouver. The Vancouver housing association made a submission to the government on rent control, of which I received a copy dated August 1949. I may say that the submission was made in view of reports circulated that it was the intention to end all controls on March 31, 1950. In part they say this:
If rent controls were necessary at the time of their imposition, they are doubly necessary now in cities with housing shortage. In Vancouver, despite the high rate of building, the shortage estimated reliably at 20,000 dwellings at the end of the war has risen by a further 5,000 during the last three years.
So that today there is a shortage of 25,000 family units. Where there is a shortage of rental dwellings this allowed increase will amount to something very drastic to people who cannot afford any further increases in their cost of living.
I have said that I know from talking with some landlords, and knowing about their circumstances, that controls worked a hardship on some. But to say that all landlords are in that position is nonsense. Hon. members know that in most of the poorer dwellings, and perhaps in most of the middle class dwellings, no repairs have been made and no decorating done in the last eight or nine years. Tenants have been doing their own repairing and decorating. With the increases now allowed, in the event of a tenant not paying the amount asked and having to move out, the landlord will have the advantage of the repairing and decorating and will increase the rent to the next tenant.
I wonder if I might be permitted to draw the attention of the house to those who are going to be affected by this change. The Vancouver housing bulletin of September, 1949, contains some specimen cases.
1. A family of seven (five children and the two parents) have an income of $112 per month, and $25 family allowance, or $137 per month. Rent for a small, dark, two-room suite in a dingy, indescribably dirty house in the Chinese section-
This is in Vancouver.
-is $47.30 per month. This leaves them $90 per month for food, clothing, fuel, light and other expenses. The low cost adequate food allowance for a family of this size-
Food allowance alone.
-is $116.

Rent Control
The hon. member who preceded me can meet these increases with equanimity. He will not feel them, but if there is another rental increase in this case there will be another reduction in the amount of food available for the children. Canada cannot build a great nation on undernourished children. Case No. 2 is as follows:
A mother with two children has an income ot $58.50 and $10 family allowance. Formerly they lived in a small housekeeping room on East Hastings, where rent was $42.50 per month. After eviction for nonpayment of rent, they moved to a room on Cordova where they pay $12 per week or $51.60 per month. This leaves them $16.90 for food and all other expenses . . .
That is, $16.90 for a mother and two children. Does my hon. friend think that an increase in rent is not important to this woman and her two children? I could read dozens of these cases. We have on the order paper amendments to the National Housing Act. I am not going to discuss them. I was about to say a great majority of the people of Canada cannot afford to pay economic rent, but I will not say that. I do not know. It is agreed that a large number of Canadian families cannot pay economic rent, and it is proposed that the building of houses shall be subsidized to enable them to pay. If that is necessary for the building of new homes, it is equally necessary for rented premises where families are not able to provide the required rent. If we were willing to do so, there could have been some sort of reasonable provision made for a much smaller rent increase than the one that has been allowed.
Let me tell the minister and hon. members of the house that these rental increases are taking place when cold weather is coming on, and in the winter it is cold in every part of Canada. Additional amounts of money are required for clothing, food and fuel, and to have a rent increase besides makes the position of these people unbearable.
This is happening at a time when residential construction is falling off, when unemployment is increasing, and when production in various lines is decreasing. Where are we going to end? Among numerous letters received, I have one I took out of my mail box as I was coming into the house. It is from the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada, British Columbia provincial command. The letter is addressed to me and reads:
Dear Mr. Maclnnis:
This provincial command wishes to again go on record as being strongly opposed to the unjust rental increases as published recently in the press. Housing shortage and unemployment are two of our major problems, and any increase in rent at this time will work a great hardship on all our citizens, particularly pensioners, war veterans allowance recipients and widows. In this regard I would ask you to place our representations before the appropriate government department.

The letter is signed "H. E. Warburton," secretary of the organization I have mentioned. I am drawing this letter to the attention not only of the department but also of the minister and hon. members of the house who know these conditions as well as I do, no matter how smugly they may sit and glower.
I said that housing construction was falling off. I have a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of October 5 giving figures as to the construction situation in the eight municipalities making up greater Montreal. The figure for last year was slightly over $10 million, and this year it is a little less than $5,900,000, a drop of nearly 50 per cent. The same situation is true in my own city.

speechtext:
Fewer starts; that is the proper word. Surely in the face of these circumstances this party is not doing a disservice to the house or to the people of Canada by bringing these matters to the attention of the house. I appreciate the difficulties associated with rent control, but there are difficulties associated with almost everything in life. I remember before coming to attend the 1948 session of the house I was asked, with a number of other men in public life including some members of parliament, to attend a meeting called by the two labour bodies of Vancouver, the Vancouver labour council and the Vancouver trades and labour council, to discuss the question of the high cost of living. I remember at that meeting one of the speakers who preceded me justifying the increases, and saying that what was required was greater production. When my turn came to speak I said that I fully agreed that what was required was greater production, but I said the moment we get greater production, overcome the present shortages and bring supply up to demand, then under our system of production for profit production will fall off. The people will be poorer than they are now, not because they did not produce enough but because they produced too much. That is the situation facing us across Canada: production increasing, poverty increasing, and the ability of the people to consume decreasing. That is the problem we have to solve, and we are not going to solve it by removing rent control. Neither are we going to solve it by imposing rent control. We can only solve it when, as the

Rent Control
hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said, we make it a part of our national objective to see that people are properly housed and properly fed. Until we do that we shall be plagued with these problems.
I could give this house figures to show how production is falling off and how unemployment is increasing. In September of this year the number of people on the unemployment insurance roll was approximately twice what it was for the same month last year, while the amount paid out in benefits was more than twice the amount paid out last year. So let us not, as the saying is, kid ourselves that we are going to remedy this situation by removing rent control. We can do that and add to the accumulated misery of increasing numbers of people in this country. Or we can do something else; by the proper use of the natural resources of this country and the skill and ability of our workers and technicians, we can build a better life in Canada for all our people.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this very important motion which has been moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and in a few words to voice the protests of my many constituents who have been seriously affected by the action of the government in permitting rent increases of from 20 to 25 per cent. This matter is causing serious concern in thousands of Canadian homes at the present time. It is causing concern to thousands of low income families, thousands of old age pensioners, thousands of people receiving small disability pensions and thousands of recipients of war veterans allowance. So I think we are fully justified in taking this time to bring to the attention of the house the plight of this large section of the Canadian people.
The arguments concerning this subject have been fully developed in this debate, so it is almost impossible for one to add a new thought; but in the few minutes I wish to speak I want to deal particularly with three points. My first point is that on this important issue, concerning which the country has been showing great anxiety for weeks and months and with which hon. members of the house have been concerned since coming to Ottawa, we are informed of government policy and government action through a statement in the house by the minister. I am of the opinion that if the government had brought this matter before the house and had permitted one day's debate on the issue before coming to a decision, and then had given effect to the opinion of a majority of hon. members, the result would
have been very different from the policy announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
My second point is that in my view there is an evasion of responsibility on the part of the government in dealing with this question. I know that technically and from the constitutional point of view property and civil rights come under the provinces. But under the conditions existing in Canada today who can say there is not a national emergency as'far as housing is concerned? More than that, the government could act on this matter with the full support of the Canadian people. The provinces are not anxious to take over this responsibility. They realize the difficulties and the magnitude of the problem. The federal government has been operating this machinery of rent control for some years now.
Mention has been made of a reference of the matter to the supreme court, and the wish has been expressed that the provinces would take responsibility in this field. I repeat that in this matter of rent control I believe the government is evading its responsibility, in view of the attitude of the Canadian people and their support for the continuation of this measure. To support that point of view I want to read briefly from a statement on rent control issued by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. Before doing so I want to point out that without question this body represents a large segment of the business interests of the country. Those who are elected as mayors and representatives of the municipalities in Canada are usually people in business, people with some assets, people who are quite levelheaded and constructive in their approach to any given question. The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities is composed of people of all political parties; and, as a previous speaker has said, this matter of rent control is not a political question. It embraces all of us; it is an economic question of serious concern to the Canadian people. To support my contention that in this matter the government is evading its responsibility I quote briefly from this statement:
For the federal government to withdraw from the field of rent controls, on the understanding that the provincial governments may step in, if they wish, would not be a solution, but rather an evasion of responsibility. To be realistic in this matter it must be recognized that for reasons of their own the provinces are not likely to enter the rent control field, at any rate in time to prevent the serious situation which will undoubtedly arise should the federal government relinquish its present controls.
I think in allowing flat increases of from 20 to 25 per cent the government is getting very close to relinquishing rent control. That was my second point. Before sitting down I want to make a third point, that the

Rent Control
increases permitted under the new order are far more drastic than were expected even by those who at times are considered to look at things from the point of view of the property owner. To support that statement, I want to quote again from this brief:
While the retention of rent controls Is imperative, no objection can be raised to permitting reasonable increases in rent levels, provided (a) they are carefully scaled and controlled and provided (b) it is recognized that the proper corollary to decontrol is a positive program of assisting low rent housing construction. Thus it might be reasonable to permit additional rent increases for residential property erected prior to 1945 of no more than 10 per cent, graduated downwards to a maximum of 5 per cent for rentals which are below $40 a month.
Before concluding that paragraph may I say that if the government had brought this question before the house and hon. members had been free to express their sincere beliefs, I believe these are possibly the increases which would have been endorsed by the House of Commons. They would have been a ten per cent increase on, shall I say, the middle class type of dwelling and a five per cent increase for the lower income group. Possibly that would have been considered and adopted by this house. I realize that in some cases landlords have been suffering an injustice. I know some people of very fine type who, out of generosity, had allowed people to live in certain quarters, during the depression and the years previous to the war, at a rental far less than economic. Then, because of their generosity, they have suffered for some years owing to these restrictions.
Continuing, Mr. Speaker, to read from the brief.
It must be recognized that the great majority of tenants who need protection against exorbitant increases are in this group; and it is this group who have not been able to find any new accommodation within their means since the war. Because of these circumstances, the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities most strongly urges upon the federal government that they reassure the people of Canada that it is not their intention to remove rent controls in March, 1950, as has been suggested by press reports.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there is no question about the attitude of the majority of the Canadian people. It is indicated by editorials in the newspapers throughout the country. It is indicated by resolutions passed by the veterans' organizations, the Canadian Legion, the army and navy veterans, all organizations of a non-political nature. They are composed of people representing all parties in Canada, but people who are living close to the problems we are discussing this evening. In addition to that, the trade unions of this country are seriously considering making further wage demands because of this
[Mr. Herridge.l
increase in the cost of living. Various women's organizations, such as the women's institute of the province of British Columbia, are deeply concerned.
I would ask the members of this house, Mr. Speaker, when this matter comes to a vote to consider not the party point of view but the interests of the Canadian people as a whole, and for once do something the majority of the Canadian people wish them to do, that is, to support the protest my leader made this afternoon.

subtopic: INCREASED RENTALS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to convey my most sincere and heartfelt congratulations to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) for the interest they have shown in the study of this problem.
In fact, they lifted the debate to the level of a social question in dealing mostly with the possible social effects of the present removal of controls. I believe it proper to follow them on this ground and to consider not only the economic aspects of the problem, as dealt with so far, but also the social aspect.
Everyone knows that each of those measures is in itself of definite and distinct social import, involving repercussions that will be felt later not unlike the ripples expanding to the edge of a pond into which a stone has been cast.
The Liberal policy has always been a social policy in the highest sense of the word. It has even reached a high degree of Christian charity. The Liberal policy in the past has never sought immediate benefits and political advantage. It has been marked by foresight and when the time came, in 1940, to set up controls that ran counter to the wishes, the aspirations and the instinctive inclinations of the Canadian people the Liberal party did not fear, at that time, to establish control of salaries, wages, rentals, etc., at all levels of social life.
The Liberal policy adopted in 1940 upset all the notions we held till then with regard to housing. We thought that the right of ownership stood solely for the proprietor's personal and immediate benefit. The Liberal policy reversed that idea, so that the tenant could have the full and real use of the property. It considered property as a commodity which could be disposed of as ordinary chattels.
The measure adopted in 1940 was a courageous one, and this more recent action by the government is also courageous and will bear fruit in the future.

The government and all the members of this house should fully realize that our housing policy must be far-reaching, taking into account not only the present but also the future.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) has just made known the government's housing program. An adjustment is taking place in labour costs. Materials are becoming increasingly plentiful. Plumbing and heating fixtures are the only materials still in somewhat short supply. This would show that a readjustment is really taking place in the country's economy and that it will become easier to solve the housing problem.
An incentive is required. Interest is still a driving power. It is useless and ill-advised to lull tenants with the belief that the government will always provide for their housing needs. The incentive lies in the substantial 20 to 25 per cent increase decreed by the government. This is a sensible measure. It shows a good appreciation of the housing situation today.
Had we continued to please tenants by granting increases of 5 to 10 per cent, they never would have faced the need of becoming property owners. The construction program which the government wishes to undertake would have met with failure without this measure of decontrol, which is but the continuation of the same courageous decision taken in the past by the government.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, this measure is an act of justice and I would add of belated justice. Rentals have been frozen for nine years. For instance, in the city of Ottawa, the rent of some controlled dwellings is $25 to $30 per month, while similar decontrolled accommodation is being rented at $60, $75 and $80. There surely is disproportion and injustice, and there has been since 1940 or 1941.
I said a while ago that our understanding of what was meant by property rights has been changed. Such rights consist in using and disposing of one's assets at will. For nine years, the plight of the property owner has been such that he could neither use nor dispose of his assets. Our whole economy in the field of rent control was based solely on the principle that rents being considered essentially as chattels, the tenant alone was entitled to use them.
The remedy introduced in 1947 was practically useless. Before regaining possession
Rent Control
of his property, the owner had to prove in court that his need was greater than the tenant's.
Again, I say that property rights had been disregarded. However, I do not wish to censure the government since rent control was providing for an emergency brought about by the war.
I believe that today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) again deserves to be congratulated.

I want to speak for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, in support of the resolution. Some hon. members have criticized the minister for the timing of this particular order in council. For the tenants who will be affected by this order, I suppose the timing is bad. This increase comes at the time of the year when living expenses are at their highest. No time of the year could be chosen when this order would be more harmful to the millions who will be affected by it and who come within the low-income brackets.
But, I take it, that was not the consideration taken into account by the minister in timing this particular order. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has shown astute political judgment in his choice of timing. I submit that he would not have gone on the hustings before June 27, nor would any member of the cabinet nor any Liberal candidate in this country, and announced the fact that they were going to "up" rents by 20 to 25 per cent. I submit that none of those same cabinet ministers or Liberal candidates would have dared to make that announcement on the eve of the recent by-elections. Coming as it does after a general election and after a series of byelections, and four years away from the next general election, it is good political timing. That consideration, I submit, was the one uppermost in the minister's mind and in the government's mind at the time this order was issued.
The minister speaks of his orderly decontrol of rent. I can understand some of the difficulties in which the minister and his associates found themselves with regard to this matter of rent and rent control. This order in council is the culmination of a series of such orders which have made a complete hodgepodge of the whole business of rent control. The government had gotten themselves into such difficulties concerning rent control that no doubt something had to

Rent Control
be done. It was becoming apparent that the job of rent control was getting just too big for the government. I suggest that the government policy of decontrol has been a disorderly rather than an orderly one. Here are some of the things that have been permitted to happen under rent control.
A few blocks from where I live, a house that was built for $8,000 in the middle thirties has, under government rent control, been sold and resold until a few days ago it sold for $22,000; and it is now rented for $175 a month whereas, prior to the war, it was renting for $55. That is the kind of thing that has been happening under the government rent control policy. There was no end of loopholes.
In the city of Toronto today there are any number of tenants who, under the government's rent control policy, are able to sublet single rooms and for those rooms collect rents that more than cover the entire rental they are paying for the house. That has been happening under the government's rent control policy.
It is true that there were some landlords who were "stuck". There were landlords who, during the depression years, were generous and conscientious enough to keep their rents down and who were caught by the government orders. Many of them have been stuck and have been obliged to rent their properties at a deflated value. Undoubtedly there are people who have suffered because they have been unable to get into some of the houses that they have purchased with the intention of moving into them. There has been a great deal of unfairness in the whole rent control business.
What was needed, I submit, was not a general lifting of rents by 20 per cent or 25 per cent, but an overhauling of the rent control regulations. There was ample room for improvement and for an overhauling. But the government did not receive from the country, on June 27, a mandate to raise rents by 20 or 25 per cent. I am going to ask this question of these Toronto Liberal members, most of whom have been in their seats all during this debate, and not one of whom has made any move to rise either to defend the government's position or to appose it. Because the minister led off in this debate by stating the government's position, are we to believe of these Toronto Liberal members -who during the campaign were so loud in telling the people of their constituencies what the government would do about the housing situation-that they took a hint from the minister's speech? The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) during the election had a great

deal to say about what this Liberal government would do with regard to the housing situation. I suppose no member in this house had more to say during that campaign than had the hon. member for Spadina about the wonderful things the Liberal government, if elected, would do to relieve the housing situation. I have not heard him protesting against these government orders.
As every Liberal and other member from Toronto knows, in the city of Toronto today the housing situation is desperate. I challenge any member elected from a Toronto or York riding to claim that he had any mandate from the people of those ridings to support a boosting of rents to 20 or 25 per cent. Just what has been the government's policy on decontrol? Let us look for a moment at how the government is gradually getting rid of control in this field. First of all, any accommodation built since January 1, 1947, is not subject to control. That lets out, I am told, about
50,000	units which have been provided since January 1, 1947, where builders and landlords have been free to squeeze out of the tenant every last dollar that the market would permit, and that has been followed pretty' generally.
Then another group became decontrolled, namely, the accommodation that has been vacated for various reasons since November 1, 1948. That lets another considerable group of houses and landlords out from under control. Under this new regulation, as I understand it, any tenant who is unwilling to take a year's lease at the increased price which the landlord may charge, up to 20 or 25 per cent as the case may be, can be ousted from his house. That is going to remove another large group from control. That appears to be the policy which the government is deliberately following in its decontrol measures.
Today I read in the press that the case which was to come before the supreme court in Toronto to determine whether or not the federal government was within its jurisdiction in maintaining controls was indefinitely postponed because the government's solicitor was not present. If that is true I want to ask this question. Has the government's last move in this respect been so agreeable to the real estate interests who were pressing this case that they are now satisfied and are we going to have a test case? We were told by the minister that every effort would be made to have this test case brought on and judgment rendered in time for the provinces to take over control should the federal government find that it could no longer maintain rent control. It would seem to me that in a matter so vital the government would see to it that its solicitor was on the job when a case of this kind came before the courts.

I turn now to a discussion of the landlords. iVe saw this afternoon how the minister's leart bled for the landlords just as another ninister's heart seemed to bleed yesterday ifternoon for the poor milling interests of this :ountry. Under the government's regulations here are unquestionably some landlords who lave suffered, and unquestionably a modifica-ion should have been made in the rental egulations to take care of these cases of njustice and unfairness. But there is a large ;roup of landlords who will derive high entals under this order, not because of any nvestment or increased investment that they lave made in their property, but because the *alue of their properties has risen along with he rising costs of other general commodities, would say that by and large the landlords ave not fared too badly, considering the arge group which has been let out com-letely from underneath controls.
It is rather interesting to find the minister
0	concerned with the landlord's side of the uestion. I want to ask him whether he has onsidered other parties who will be affected.
submit that if the minister has given per-lission to landlords to raise the rents of those 'ho are on old age pension, of veterans who re subsisting on their pensions and on eterans' allowances, then he is in duty ound, as far as these same people are con-erned, to increase their pensions and their Uowances by an equal amount.
The minister's action will be the beginning f a whole series of demands across this auntry for wage increases. Over the week ad I had the privilege of meeting representa-ves of about thirty trade union locals. The leeting was called to discuss a certain subset. That whole meeting resolved itself spon-meously into a protest on the part of the ade unionists present against the government's action of raising rents. The one thing lat was emphasized all through this meeting as the determination of those who were Seers of trade union locals to press on the rst opportunity for wage increases in order
1	compensate the workers for the increases i rent which they would be required to pay. This evening the Ottawa Journal carries a sading that the increase in rent sparks a jmand on the part of civil servants for creased salaries. This morning the Montreal azette carried the story of the president of ie dominion civil servants association, aiming that that organization would be ireed to seek higher salaries to offset ie increases in rent which the civil rvants would be required to pay. That is >t a good thing for this country at this time, ut the government could not have made any her one single move that would have
Rent Control
sparked trade unions across this country, civil servants and others, to go out immediately to demand increased wages.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that this debate does not give every hon. member an opportunity to show by his vote just where he stands on this issue. I am sure that some of the good Liberals from the Toronto ridings would find it very difficult to cast a vote in this house in support of the measure. I want to ask them, in closing, what voice they had as members of the government party in determining or helping to determine this policy which the government has announced. I ask that because during the election campaign the Liberal condidates in Toronto were constantly telling us how much more beneficial it would be for the people of Toronto if they had members sitting on the government benches. I ask those member who are on the government benches tonight what they are doing for their constituents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much has been said about rent controls. I have very little to add, except a reply to an hon. member on the government side of the house who suggested that the country is behind the action taken by the government in increasing rents. Let me point out to him that the federation of mayors who met recently in Montreal were most emphatic in their views on rent control. I consider this one of the best bodies in Canada, from the standpoint of gauging public opinion. In it are the mayors of every town across this dominion. They are closely associated with the people in those towns, and their interests are closer to those of the people than the interests of members of parliament here in Ottawa.
Let me quote what they have to say with regard to controls. They say, in part:
As such, it has no hesitation in saying that the removal of all rent controls, now or in the near future, would produce catastrophic effects for thousands of families throughout the country, and more particularly in those cities where there continues to be a demonstrably large housing shortage.
I would include in those towns both Ottawa and Montreal. Not a single member, to my knowledge, has risen in his place to protest against the condition which will arise in those cities when rents are increased. The statement from the mayors continues:
It needs no argument to show that the inflation of prices since 1946, particularly affecting real estate, has shot the level of rents for new dwellings out of all comparison with the rents which prevailed over large areas of Canadian cities before the war.
Then, referring to the general shortage of homes they go on to say:
Until this glaring weakness in the national housing program is rectified, a prospect which is not likely for the near future, it would be a dereliction of responsibility for the government to withdraw from the rental control field.

Rent Control
Then they go on to give an example. It continues:
No less disturbing Is the acute sense of insecurity already engendered in the minds of thousands^ of tenants by the mere rumour of decontrol, giving rise to the fear of evictions as well as that of having to pay rent beyond their means.
I suggest that those are the true views of the common people of Canada, and not the views as expressed by hon. members who would support the government in what it has done. The mayors are fair in the suggestion they make. They suggest, as did the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), that a fair increase is due and reasonable, and would be acceptable. Their suggestion is a general increase of 10 per cent and an increase of 5 per cent on low-rental housing, not exceeding $40 a month. With that I would agree. I feel the capital invested in many of the homes now increasing in rents has not been changed for twenty years. It is the original capital. I admit that capital has shown good returns for ten or twenty years; but the same capital today is showing greater
returns than it ever did from the inception of the investments, because today the same homes and tenements are in full occupancy,
Already they have been given three increases in rents, and many of the services they formerly gave to tenants are not being given. They are cutting down on repairs, heating and in every way grasping that extra dollar which can be obtained from lowered services. I feel that, in protest against giving these people an added 20 per cent, the condemnation of the whole country has beer voiced by the federation of mayors on behall of the common people of Canada.

speechtext:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, November 7, 1949
My dear Premier:
I wish to advise you that I have now heard from the premiers of all the provinces, and that Tuesday, January 19, 1950, appears to be generally acceptable as a date for the opening session of the dominion-provincial conference to consider a method of amending the constitution of Canada. It is therefore proposed to open the conference in Ottawa at 10.30 a.m. on that date.
As many of the premiers did not feel that a preliminary meeting of constitutional experts in advance of the main conference would serve any useful purpose, my colleagues and I feel we should not attempt to arrange such a meeting.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent
Wednesday, November 9, 1949
